holds: free guides, ebooks, offices to rent; ads and buttons
fails: where the benefit was added to the offer instead of replacing it, the two together won (Boys Town +55.6%)
rule: Say plainly what people get; in cold ads the plain offer beats the promise and the fright.
result: "Get the Guide" +44.7% over "Detect Breast Cancer Earlier"; "Get this free resource" +45.6% over "At Risk for Cancer?"; "Get eBook" +49.2% sign-ups over "Learn how"; "Get the free ebook" +10.8%; "Get" vs "Order" +38.26%; "Get the free book" vs "Download" +133.7%
measured_by: NextAfter (samples 1,250 to 75,724) and Michael Aagaard, separate A/B tests
how_to_use: write the benefit, then the plain offer with "get": "Effectively discipline your tween – get the free email series"
source: NextAfter experiments; Unbounce

fails: sometimes both move together (rehab headline: clicks +400%, leads +26%)
rule: An opening that wins clicks can lose the sale: judge by the last step.
result: "Learn how" won clicks (+43.2%) and lost sign-ups to "Get eBook" (+49.2%); $50-off and 15%-off mails had equal opens (20% / 19%) and clicks, yet $50-off brought 170% more revenue; "191 articles" banner +24% clicks, donations about the same
measured_by: NextAfter N 6,616; Evo e-mail split; Wikimedia 1.17 million impressions per arm
how_to_use: never crown a hook on stops or clicks alone; write down the next step's number
source: MarketingSherpa (Evo); NextAfter; Wikimedia

fails: Luther Seminary: with an unknown person the organisation's name alone opened better (+13.1%)
rule: A named person speaking beats a slogan; their own spoken words beat the polished version.
result: Jimmy Wales appeal 3.68% clicks and 62 gifts vs at most 0.25% and 5 for slogans; Kaldari word-for-word letter 126 vs 96 donations; Harvest mail that looked personally sent +116%; Highrise customer photo page +47% paid sign-ups
measured_by: Wikimedia 2010-11; NextAfter N 123,249; 37signals
how_to_use: interview the owner or a customer on tape and open with a sentence as spoken
source: Wikimedia Foundation, Fundraising 2011 test updates

holds: a shared service used by very many
fails: money per impression: the deadline came close or ahead on single days
rule: Asking everyone for a tiny sum brings twice the givers of a deadline, with smaller gifts.
result: "If everyone reading this donated $5": 590 gifts vs 277 for "Only 4 days left" on 2.7 million impressions each; with $10 instead of $5: 192 vs 243 gifts, money about equal
measured_by: Wikimedia Foundation December 2010
how_to_use: name a small sum and what it adds up to; run the deadline only in the last days, and only a true one
source: Wikimedia Foundation, Fundraising 2010 banner testing

holds: free services asking for voluntary support
fails: not tested for selling goods; organ donor page: "thousands decide to register" won over the plain request
rule: "Almost nobody does this" can beat "everybody does this" when you ask people to carry something they use.
result: removing "99% of readers don’t give" lowered the donation rate in dozens of tests; CBN article appeal with "fewer than 1%" +77.1%; FamilyLife "3%" line +84.2%
measured_by: Wikimedia dozens of tests; NextAfter N 759,079 and 64,667
how_to_use: use it for tip jars, memberships, reviews; not for products
source: Wikimedia Foundation, 2018-19 report

fails: real customer photos raised sales (37signals +47%)
rule: A stock photo can turn a good line into a bad one.
result: "Every day thousands…" +0.6 points alone; with a group stock photo below the control
measured_by: Behavioural Insights Team, RCT, over 135,000 people per variant
how_to_use: no picture is better than a stock group; use the real owner or customer
source: Behavioural Insights Team 2013

fails: Aagaard: similar tests in Danish did not work; in the WriteWork test "my" lost
rule: Put the reader's own voice on the button (my, yes I), where the language allows it.
result: "Get my free 30-day trial" +90% clicks; "your" on a payment page -24.95%; "Yes, I can give $25" +32.5% donations; "Make my Gift" +74% donations while "Donate Today!" -6%
measured_by: Michael Aagaard; NextAfter N 113,294 and 3,092
how_to_use: test "my" once per language before making it a habit
source: MarketingExperiments, on Michael Aagaard's talk

fails: not tested for paid goods
rule: "Activate" beats "Learn more" and "Enroll" for something free: it sounds already yours.
measured_by: NextAfter, three organisations
how_to_use: say "activate / switch on your free …" when nothing has to be bought
source: NextAfter

fails: for proof of how many customers, big exact numbers won (172,783+: sales +26.8%)
rule: A small number people can picture beats a huge one.
result: "Allow 36 More Couples" 2.4% vs "Reach 7,000 more people" 1.2%; "720 women" +19.2% opens; "just a few gifts short" +64.6% donations
how_to_use: small number for the effect of one buyer, big exact number for the crowd of buyers
source: NextAfter

holds: health plans, car repair, planners, b2b
fails: National Breast Cancer popup: the general "Help Women Facing Breast Cancer" beat "1,000 more women" (+14.3%, N 144,374)
rule: Exact figures in the headline win over adjectives.
result: "$8.33 a month" +72.76%, "Over 55,000" +26.41%, best of six; "in Just One Hour" +58%; "172,783+" +26.8% sales; "Over 120,000 Doctors" +104% clicks; "7 proven methods" +770.7%
measured_by: MarketingExperiments, SplitBase, NextAfter; N mostly not given
how_to_use: put the price, the time or the count in the first line, and test it once against the human line
source: MarketingExperiments 2006

fails: a reader-centred question can win (Do your landing pages pass this test? +125.9% clicks)
rule: Writing about yourself in the headline loses to writing about the reader's result.
result: "Why do 10,000 Event Planners Choose RegOnline?" lost to "Let Your Events Manage Themselves" (+90%); "Why Try Britannica Online?" lost (+103%); "We’re here to help." lost (+638% leads)
measured_by: MECLABS tests collected in 2019; N not given
how_to_use: delete the company from the first line; ask questions only about the reader
source: MarketingExperiments; MarketingSherpa blog 2019

fails: small counts
rule: The last line can kill the first: two clever words added cost every lead.
result: "…FIVE MILLION separate documents." 9 leads of 948; the same plus "And smile." 0 leads of 888
measured_by: MarketingExperiments split run 2006
how_to_use: cut the joke at the end of a working line
source: MarketingExperiments 2006

fails: mystery won where the mail itself was the gift (Coming tomorrow +13.3%)
rule: Subject lines: say exactly what it is, as a person would; curiosity opens more but often does not sell more.
result: "A free copywriting training class for you" +41.9% clicks; "A new year-end fundraising webinar for you" +42.7%; "Download our latest eBook" +51.3%; "Matt, I’ve been working on this for you" +25.5% opens with no more sign-ups; open loop +18.3% opens with lower click-through
measured_by: NextAfter, N 7,814 to 39,673
how_to_use: use plain + "for you" when you need the click, mystery only when the open itself is the goal
source: NextAfter

fails: honest mystery elsewhere won
rule: Misleading curiosity raises opens once and costs trust.
result: subject about Alfred Hitchcock +12.7% opens; the authors state they will never use it again; the pure curiosity line came last of six
measured_by: MarketingExperiments / MECLABS tests 2012
how_to_use: a curious line must be paid off in the first sentence
source: MarketingExperiments 2012

holds: requests to people who already use you
fails: Wikipedia 2023 retest null
rule: Asking modestly ("if it's not too much to ask", "humbly") lifted gifts; it wears off once the whole text is humble.
measured_by: NextAfter two organisations; Wikimedia Foundation
how_to_use: use one modest phrase in the ask for a review, a referral, a deposit
source: Wikipedia:Fundraising/2023 banners; NextAfter

fails: 2 of 10 country tests went the other way
rule: Name the reader's own place in the first words.
result: country in the first line: 11% more likely to donate, 8 of 10 significant tests positive; "Find gym" added to the button +68%
measured_by: Wikimedia 2015-16; Michael Aagaard
how_to_use: street, quarter or town in the first five words of a local ad
source: Wikimedia Foundation 2015-16

holds: daily messages to the same people
fails: one-time ads to strangers not tested
rule: Winners wear out: a new wording gets a lift just for being new, so keep several and rotate.
result: new push templates tended to raise response even when not better in the long run; rotating by freshness gave +0.5% daily active users and +2% new-user retention
measured_by: Duolingo, live test on millions of daily reminders (Yancey & Settles, KDD 2020)
how_to_use: keep at least five proven openings per channel and rest each after use
source: Duolingo KDD 2020

doubt: page wording filtered by machine; median lifts are of winners only and overstate
holds: all kinds of page and mail tests
fails: published archive, so failures may be missing on top
rule: Half of all A/B tests prove nothing, even in a professional shop.
result: 3,947 published experiments: 2,015 valid at 95%; a treatment beat the control in 1,488 of those
measured_by: NextAfter archive, counted by me from the saved pages
how_to_use: plan the sample before the test; throw away any win without one
source: NextAfter experiment library

doubt: grouped by words in the page address; small groups
fails: shops: exact crowd numbers won (SELF Journal +26.8%, daFlores +44%)
rule: Testimonials and "many people" lines win less often than clear wording.
result: in valid tests a treatment won: clarity 73 of 93, subject lines 93 of 117, headlines 36 of 42; social proof 9 of 15, testimonials 7 of 12, with median lifts 9.6% and 14.7%
measured_by: NextAfter archive counted by me
how_to_use: fix clarity first, add proof second
source: NextAfter experiment library

rule: Experts guess wrong about which opening wins; test instead of voting.
result: 89% of 135 marketers voted for the ad texts that did worst; 74.76% of the clinic audience picked a losing headline; the CEO's own headline lost by 92%; Obama staff favoured the video that lost
measured_by: AdEspresso $1,000 test; MarketingExperiments; Optimizely
how_to_use: let the numbers choose between at least three openings
source: AdEspresso; MarketingExperiments; Optimizely

holds: a free ebook to a lookalike audience, US
fails: one offer, one audience; result tables are pictures
rule: Facebook ads: too short costs leads, and no button costs more.
result: medium to long ad texts had the lowest cost per lead; worst text 2.4 times the best; no button nearly 2.5 times the cost; "Download" was the best of four buttons
measured_by: AdEspresso, $1,000 each, 7 texts ($142.90 each) and 4 buttons ($250 each)
how_to_use: write one full paragraph before trying one-liners; name the act on the button
source: AdEspresso

fails: clicks only
rule: In search ads write in sentence case, not every word capitalised.
result: 9 of 12 ad sets with only the first word capitalised had higher click-through, 6% to 64% higher
measured_by: ORYX Rent a Car, three-month A/B test, 12 sets
how_to_use: drop Title Case in ads and test once
source: MarketingSherpa quick case study #7

fails: small second sample
rule: A thank-you page is an opening too: "Thank you" reads as "you may go".
result: headline that announced the mail and then asked a question: donations +75.8% (N 4,612); DTS without the confirmation headline 13.2% vs 6.4% (N 446)
measured_by: NextAfter
how_to_use: after an order, say what happens next and ask one thing
source: NextAfter

fails: samples mostly not given
rule: Say the word the customer uses, not the trade's.
result: "Annual Reports" vs "SEC Filings" +26% leads; "Request Pricing" vs "Request a Quote" +95% clicks; adding "supplement" +89.97% purchases; "create a page" vs "create a site" +151.4%; "Monthly Support" vs "Give with Impact" +157.1% clicks
measured_by: MECLABS, One Call Now, VWO/Movexa, NextAfter
how_to_use: list the trade words on the page and swap them one by one
source: NextAfter; MarketingSherpa; VWO

holds: asking for money for a shared good; warm, frequent users
fails: headlines and buttons: shorter often won there (JumpBox six words to four, 87.61%)
rule: In long personal appeals, cutting the text to a tidy short line destroys the result.
result: one-line donate banner: 95% drop in donation rate; a single good paragraph: -35% donations per impression; mobile banner twice as long: +40%; long Harvest ad value text +316%
measured_by: Wikimedia Foundation live tests 2017-2025; NextAfter N 710,592
how_to_use: keep the first line short, let the body tell the whole story under it
source: Wikipedia:Fundraising/2024 banners (Wikimedia staff report)

rule: Fill the empty product page: a clear list of what it is, what it does and when you use it sold 6.5 % more — but only where the old text was under 50 words.
result: Sales +2.1 % over 4.77 million shoppers (p<.05); products with no or under 50 words of text +6.5 %; products already well described: no effect. Returns −3.9 % (p<.01). Conversion up, basket size unchanged.
measured_by: Fang, Yuan, Donati, Zhang, Sarvary (2026): RANDOMISED shoppers on a huge cross-border shop, one week Dec 2023, about 45,000 products
holds: cross-border marketplace, text bullets added above the old text
fails: AI text, so wording and completeness changed together; well-written pages gain nothing
how_to_use: First job for any shop client: 5 bullets (feature, benefit, use) on every thin page, before any clever hook.
source: Fang, Yuan, Donati, Zhang, Sarvary, Generative AI and Sales Productivity, arXiv 2510.12049v6, June 2026
doubt: short term; the firm employed one author; the 6.5 % split is English only

rule: Selling a repeat purchase: say what it does for them (never running out, a reminder) next to the discount. Discount alone wins fewer sign-ups and loses them sooner.
result: Messages with a non-price benefit beat price-only on sign-ups AND on staying. Model: moving everyone from price-only to the reminder message for one month = +968 subscribers and +$155,000 (+6.1 %) subscription revenue.
measured_by: Kalyanam, Thomadsen, Zhao 2025 (SSRN 5338643): four-week RANDOMISED e-mail field experiment at a major pet-products retailer; the 968 / $155k are a counterfactual calculation; N not seen
holds: subscription to physical goods, customers who already bought online
fails: abstract only; not one hook isolated; not repeated
how_to_use: 'Never run out of Bella's food again' first, '10 % off every refill' second.
source: Kalyanam, Thomadsen, Zhao, The Impact of Advertising Content on Customer Acquisition and Retention for Subscriptions of Physical Goods, SSRN, July 2025
doubt: abstract read from a search answer; full paper closed (SSRN and WashU refused)

rule: At the moment of PAYING, finish your sentence: a teaser cut off mid-sentence sold almost half as much as the same teaser ending in a full sentence.
result: Real purchases with vouchers: 13 of 71 (18.3 %) bought after the unfinished teaser, 24 of 72 (33.3 %) after the finished one (p=.039): about 45 % fewer sales. Faces turned negative at the pay screen (valence −11 → −25). Intention to buy lower in text (1.13 vs 1.40) and in video (1.67 vs 2.27, p=.057).
measured_by: Mandler et al., Psychology & Marketing 2024: RANDOMISED; study 1 N=143 with real money-like vouchers (€0.50 each); study 2 N=56 faces; 3a N=279; 3b N=179 video; 4 N=400 pre-registered
holds: paid digital content, students and Prolific, text and video
fails: one real-purchase study, in a lab, small N — authors warn against trusting the size
how_to_use: Ad leading straight to a price: full sentence, full promise. Never 'It soon became obvious that…' before a checkout.
source: Mandler, Cziehso, Schaefers, Kupfer, Mafael, Consumer reactions to unfinished teasers, Psychology & Marketing 2024

rule: The biggest proven wording gain: let a model that has learned from thousands of past A/B pairs (worse line → better line) rewrite the human's subject line. Plain ChatGPT does nothing.
result: 36 new e-mail campaigns, 283 million sends: clicks 0.555 % (human) → 0.729 % (+32 %, better in 35 of 36); ChatGPT-assisted 0.550 % (no difference, p=.75). Of 1,000 clicks you would have had, you get 1,320.
measured_by: Angelopoulos (Persado), Lee, Misra: RANDOMISED in each campaign; trained on 20,000 past campaigns, 286,000 subject lines, 337 brands; a human picked the final line in both AI arms. Clicks, not sales. Not yet repeated by others.
fails: 2023-era models; one author works at Persado, the seller of such a service; newer general models not tested
how_to_use: Build the pair bank (worse line, better line, same campaign); gains already strong with about 370 experiments; keep the human line in the race and let the score choose.
source: Angelopoulos, Lee, Misra, Causal Alignment: Augmenting Language Models with A/B Tests, working paper (leekevin.io/caLM.pdf)
doubt: vendor co-author; the model arms had four times the sends of the control

rule: People cannot pick the winner: shown two headlines whose real difference was proven, students were right half the time, the heaviest news readers no better.
result: 45.22 % correct (202 people, 3,809 answers) and 51.58 % (339 people, 4,571 answers); chance 50 %. Daily news readers 42.35 % and 47.48 %.
measured_by: Ye, Yoganarasimhan, Zheng, LOLA 2024, web appendix A; pairs drawn from 39,158 significantly different RANDOMISED pairs. Repeated with journalists (Shulman 2024: 50 %).
fails: readers are a decade newer than the tests
how_to_use: Never let the client's taste (or ours) choose the line; let the traffic choose.
source: Ye, Yoganarasimhan, Zheng, LOLA, arXiv 2406.02611v3, 2024

rule: People who write for a living guess the winner no better than a coin.
result: 147 journalists and writers (average 13.9 years' experience) picked the Washington Post winner in 3.09 of 6 pairs (50 %).
measured_by: Shulman et al. 2024, study 4; agrees with LOLA's students (45–52 %)
fails: six pairs only
how_to_use: Say it to the client before the first meeting about taste.
source: Shulman et al. 2024

rule: No checklist of words can tell you which of two headlines will win: at best 58 right out of 100. Test instead.
result: A model built only on word rules picks the winner in 54.42 % of 24,333 pairs; on the pairs with the biggest click difference the peak is 58.3 %. Five times more training data did not raise it.
measured_by: Gligorić et al. 2023, held-out confirmatory set, RANDOMISED A/B pairs. Repeated by Hagar et al. on Chartbeat data (cited there): modest performance above baseline.
fails: richer models do better: see LOLA and HypotheSAEs rows
how_to_use: Use word rules to widen the drafts, never to choose the final one.
source: Gligorić et al., PLOS ONE 2023

rule: Do not stop a test when it looks won: looking seven times and stopping at the first 'significant' invents a winner 16 times in 100 instead of 5.
result: False winners in identical-arm streams: 16.32 % with seven looks at 5 %, 5.03 % with one final look, 0.0 % with the always-valid method (mSPRT).
measured_by: Ushno, pre-registered preprint Nov 2026: 200,000 simulated A/A streams at the archive's real sizes
fails: simulation; one author
how_to_use: Fix the number of views before the start, or use a bandit/always-valid test. Never 'it is ahead, let us stop'.
source: Ushno, Peeking, Pooling, and a Locked Split, Zenodo, v2, 16 Nov 2026

rule: 'Posts with X got more engagement' tells you almost nothing about what X does: compared with real tests, such studies point the WRONG WAY 20 to 50 times in 100.
result: 50 wording features, two archives. Upworthy (7,797 tests): wrong direction 20 %, 34 % of real effects missed. Chartbeat (153,787 tests, 416,009 headlines, 398 news outlets): wrong direction 50 %, correlation of the two methods −0.19, 42 % false alarms. Topic controls, site controls and embeddings did not repair it.
measured_by: Banerjee & Urminsky, March 2026 preprint; RANDOMISED tests compared with simulated observational studies on the same headlines
fails: one preprint; per-feature table only in the supplement
how_to_use: Mark every 'we analysed 10,000 posts' claim (vendor or academic) as an idea to test, never as proof to a client.
source: Banerjee & Urminsky, Correlational estimates of language effects are biased…, PsyArXiv h8wvg, 2026
doubt: preprint

rule: Repeat the headline's own words on the button. The same promise in the same words gets a third more people to press it than a new argument.
result: Pressed the button: verbatim repeat 58 % (N=237), same idea in other words 48 % (N=234), a new argument 44 % (N=485). The same button text with a non-matching headline lost, so it is the match, not the words (OR 1.59).
measured_by: Kutzner, Ermark, Fornoff, Wänke, Frontiers in Psychology 2024: RANDOMISED landing pages of a real German cleaning-service site, 956 visitors, 3 weeks. Click to the next step, not a booking.
fails: not repeated; only the zip-code step
how_to_use: Ad line = page headline = button, word for word ('without stress' … 'without stress').
source: Kutzner et al., Effects of verbatim repetition of the headline message on the proceed button, Frontiers in Psychology 15:1187798, 2024

rule: Subject lines matter more than you think: in an average campaign the best one gets 73 % more than the worst.
result: Best against worst subject line within a campaign: +73 % on average, up to +445 %.
measured_by: Angelopoulos, Lee, Misra: 20,000 RANDOMISED campaigns, typically 16 lines each, median 798,000 recipients
fails: maximum over 16 lines is inflated by chance
how_to_use: Write 16 lines, not 2.
source: Angelopoulos, Lee, Misra, Causal Alignment

rule: Little traffic: let the score decide. More traffic: let the live test take over, moving views to the line that is winning instead of splitting evenly to the end.
result: Total clicks of score + live adaptive test against a classic even-split A/B: +8.69 % at 50 views per line, +5.08 % at 1,000 views per line. Against the score alone: +0.09 % at 50, +5.02 % at 1,000. Adaptive test alone against even split: +1.6 to +3.0 %.
measured_by: LOLA 2024, replay SIMULATION on held-out RANDOMISED tests; not run live
fails: no revenue measured (authors say so)
how_to_use: Under about 200 views per line do not bother testing evenly; run a bandit with the score as the head start.
source: Ye, Yoganarasimhan, Zheng, LOLA 2024, Table 7
doubt: simulation

rule: Asking a chatbot which line is best is barely better than a coin; a model trained on real test results is better, but still wrong more than half the time among four lines.
result: Finding the best of about 4: chance 33.0 %, GPT-4 asked directly 37.9–40.0 %, embeddings + simple regression 46.3 %, fine-tuned Llama-3-8B 46.9 %, fine-tuned GPT-4o 48.8 %. Wrong example answers hurt as little as right ones helped.
measured_by: LOLA 2024: 17,681 RANDOMISED tests, 77,245 headlines, 277 million impressions; held-out 3,263 tests
fails: newer models do better on clear-cut pairs (Maiorano 2026)
how_to_use: Use a trained scorer to throw out the worst drafts and to set the starting weights of the test.
source: Ye, Yoganarasimhan, Zheng, LOLA 2024

rule: Do not let an untrained AI 'improve' shopping-ad titles: the seller's own keyword-stuffed titles got more.
result: AI-optimised Google Shopping titles: views −7.7 %, clicks −10.3 %, sales −4.5 % (the sales drop not significant).
measured_by: Fang et al. 2026: RANDOMISED 1.24 million products, 12 days, Jan 2024
fails: AI not trained for ads; a trained one might differ
how_to_use: Keep buyers' search words first in the title ('2024 New Arrival Polarized … Sunglasses Men Cycling').
source: Fang et al. 2026, App. A
doubt: reason given is the authors' guess

rule: Training the ad-writing AI on real click results lifts Facebook ad clicks by 6.7 % over an AI that only imitates good-looking ads.
result: Advertiser-level CTR 3.1 % → 3.3 % (+6.7 %, p=.0296); advertisers also made 18.5 % more variations.
measured_by: Meta (Jiang, Nikulkov et al.), RANDOMISED at advertiser level: 34,849 US advertisers, 640,000 ad variations, 10 weeks Feb–Apr 2024. Clicks, not conversions (authors say conversions were too noisy).
fails: p just under .03; comparison is against a weaker AI, not against humans; own product
how_to_use: Give every ad 5 text variations and let delivery choose; feed results back into the writer.
source: Jiang et al., Improving Generative Ad Text on Facebook using RL, arXiv 2507.21983v2, Dec 2025

rule: Many different push messages instead of one for all: more orders, fewer returns, but no proven rise in money.
result: 2.7 million message variants vs about 2,000 human ones: conversion and number of orders up (significant), sales +1.6 % (not significant), returns −11.4 % (p<.01). Only 40 % of the treated group saw the AI messages.
measured_by: Fang et al. 2026: RANDOMISED, 13.7 million shoppers, one day
fails: sales effect not proven; wording not isolated
how_to_use: Vary the line per product and shopper instead of one campaign line; measure orders and returns.
source: Fang et al. 2026

rule: An e-mail title that tells the theme of what is inside brings more taps inside the mail; it did not bring more buyers.
result: Over a million users: item taps inside the mail +23.6 % (significant), opens +0.46 % (not), buyers overall −0.42 % (nothing). Control title: ''Nike Sneakers 28cm' and other items are currently on sale right now'.
measured_by: Mercari (Jobson et al., Sept 2025): RANDOMISED, over one million lapsed users, one week; buying measured and flat
fails: sales; send rate fell 0.9 %
how_to_use: Judge subject lines by buyers per target, not by taps.
source: Jobson et al., Using item recommendations and LLMs in marketing email titles, arXiv 2508.20024, 2025

rule: Tell enough to be understood, keep one thing back: the very vague headline gains from a concrete detail, the very complete one gains from losing one.
result: Among the vaguest tests the more concrete headline gets about 5.5 % more clicks (0.91 vs 0.86 %); among the most concrete tests the less concrete one gets about 10 % more (1.17 vs 1.06 %). Only 8.7 % of tests were 'too vague'; 50.9 % were 'too concrete'; in the middle 40 % it made no difference.
measured_by: Aubin Le Quéré & Matias, registered report: 8,977 RANDOMISED tests, 35,910 headlines, same image; concreteness score checked against 176 people (r = 0.61). Pilot of 2,335 tests gave the same result.
fails: the site's readers may prefer vagueness; 5.5 % / 9.9 % are the extreme ends, not the average
how_to_use: If the draft could describe any product, add a thing or a name. If nothing is left to learn, remove the last detail.
source: Aubin Le Quéré & Matias, When curiosity gaps backfire, Scientific Reports 15:994, 2025

rule: Title as a statement beats title as a question, on Reddit, in science journals and in real headline tests.
result: Four studies, same direction: 53,030 Reddit posts, 3,078,791 academic titles, 22,743 online headline experiments, pre-registered lab N=400; reason: question titles seem to contain less information. Size not printed in the open abstract.
measured_by: Fang & Wheeler, Journal of Consumer Psychology 2026; part randomised (A/B, lab), part observational. Repeated: Ushno 2026 pre-registered (−13.5 % odds), Movva 2025, Banerjee & Urminsky, Molina, Jung.
fails: Facebook brand posts: a question brings comments; TikTok like-rate 0.036 (middle of the pack); Lai & Farbrot 2014 found one positive field result
how_to_use: Answer it in the headline: 'Green tea has health benefits', not 'Does green tea…?'. Ask only where you want replies.
source: Fang & Wheeler, Titles framed as questions reduce reader engagement, JCP, 9 July 2026
doubt: abstract only; full text closed

rule: Question headlines lost clicks again on data nobody had looked at: about 13–14 fewer clicks per 100.
result: Pooled odds ratio 0.8645 (95 % CI 0.8335–0.8966), 465 tests; but very uneven between tests (I² 75.8 %): in some tests the question wins.
measured_by: Ushno 2026, pre-registered, locked split of the Upworthy archive, RANDOMISED tests; a replication of Fang & Wheeler
fails: same single publisher; the same paper finds that matched observational estimates CAN land near the truth on one site — milder than Banerjee & Urminsky
how_to_use: Statement first; a question only as one test arm.
source: Ushno, Zenodo preprint v2, 16 Nov 2026

rule: Talk about one person (I, she, he); do not talk about 'we'.
result: Win/lose logit per headline pair: I/my +0.24 (p=6e-14), she/he/it +0.22 (p=4e-19), they +0.09, we/our/us −0.15 (p=2e-5), you +0.05 (not supported at p<.01). In shop words [mine, from the logit]: of 100 pairs where only one headline says 'I', that one wins about 56; 'she/he' about 55; 'we' only about 46.
measured_by: Gligorić, Lifchits, West, Anderson, pre-registered registered report; 24,333 headline pairs, same story + same image, randomised readers (Upworthy 2013-15). RANDOMISED, clicks only, not reading or buying. Repeated: pilot set of 5,048 pairs gave the same sign for I and she/he; 'we' was not significant in the pilot.
fails: 'you' failed; no purchases measured; not repeated on TikTok (Nadia: own-account talk loses)
how_to_use: Put one named or pictured person in the subject of the first line; strike 'we/our' from the opening and say it as I or as the customer's own story.
source: Gligorić et al., Linguistic effects on news headline success, PLOS ONE 18(3) e0281682, 2023
doubt: one publisher; several things differ between the two headlines of a pair; 'it/its' is counted inside the she/he group

rule: A headline about what one other person did is the strongest wording lever of the 36 tested; speaking to the reader ('you', 'we') backfires.
result: One standard deviation more 'one person' language (he/she/social words): about +6.4 % clicks, twice the size of anything else. 'Writer to reader' (we/you) −0.000459, about −2.9 % [mine, over mean 1.6 %]. Most other levers: −3.1 % to +3.1 %.
measured_by: Banerjee & Urminsky, January 2021 draft: 3,346 randomised Upworthy tests, 14,975 headlines, three statistical corrections. RANDOMISED, clicks. Agrees with Gligorić (he/she +, we −, you ~0).
fails: draft on exploratory data; the 2024 final text could not be opened and the authors warn results may differ
how_to_use: Tell what she/he did; leave 'you' for the offer line.
source: Banerjee & Urminsky, The Language That Drives Engagement, draft Jan 2021 (final: Marketing Science 44(3), 2025)
doubt: exploratory draft, authors ask not to cite; final version not opened

rule: Put a digit in the line, and write it as a digit (3), not as a word (three) and not as 'several'.
result: Clicks +3.6 % at the Washington Post and +5.2 % at Upworthy for headlines with a digit. Lab, same headline with only the number form changed: stated chance of reading 3.44 (digit) vs 3.28 (word) vs 3.22 ('several') on a 1–6 scale; memory for the headline also better (d' 0.92 vs 0.75/0.77). In a shop: out of 1,000 clicks you get 36–52 more.
measured_by: Peters, Markowitz, Shoots-Reinhard, Ely 2026: 7,371 WaPo tests (19,926 headlines), 22,664 Upworthy tests (105,551 headlines) — randomised tests but digits not the planned change; plus pre-registered RANDOMISED lab experiment N=765 where only the number form changed. Clicks and stated intent, not buying. Repeated across two newsrooms, one lab, and the authors' two earlier social-media studies.
fails: effect is small (d 0.07–0.10); many or complicated numbers; amounts of money lose on Upworthy (Banerjee & Urminsky; first-round measurement)
how_to_use: One digit, up front: '3 drawers', '20 minutes', '41 bottles'. No big font needed for it.
source: Peters et al., Numerals in news headlines, Scientific Reports 2026 (accepted 19 Oct 2026)
doubt: press version; small effect; WaPo data not public

rule: What wins in pairs of the best and worst headline: something to look at (photo, picture), an embarrassing or uncomfortable scene, being surprised or unprepared, one woman's own journey, a video, an unexpected act. What loses: praise of a good initiative, the environment, 'we all must', a question to the reader, politicians.
result: Change in the chance of being the better one: photo/image +26 points, discomfort or embarrassment +16, surprised/shocked/unprepared +16, female subject and her journey +14, video +13, unexpected action +13, male subject +11, look/see +9, superlative/unique +9, standing up to an offence +9; politicians −10, question to reader −12, collective responsibility −13, environment −15, initiatives that help the community −16.
measured_by: Movva, Peng, Garg, Kleinberg, Pierson (ICML 2025): pairs (highest vs lowest CTR) from 14,128 RANDOMISED Upworthy tests; 15 of 20 ideas survived Bonferroni on 4,400 unseen pairs; overall AUC 0.69. Clicks only. Agrees with Banerjee & Urminsky, Gligorić and Fang.
fails: comparing best with worst exaggerates size; several features are rare (AUC 0.51 for photos)
how_to_use: Write the customer's awkward moment ('She hid her hands in every photo') instead of the good deed.
source: Movva et al., Sparse Autoencoders for Hypothesis Generation, ICML 2025, Table 1
doubt: address taken from memory of the paper, the PDF on disk was read

rule: One bad-news word lifts clicks a little; one happy word lowers them a little.
result: Each negative word in a 15-word headline: CTR +2.3 %; each positive word: −1.0 %. (If 1,000 people used to click, one negative word brings about 23 more.)
measured_by: Robertson et al., registered report: 12,448 usable randomised tests, 53,699 headlines, 205 million impressions, 2,778,124 clicks. RANDOMISED; clicks, not buying. Repeated with three sentiment dictionaries, without image tests, and in Gligorić's registered report (negative +0.18; positive −0.04 not significant).
fails: positive-word harm is not confirmed by Gligorić; sharing and shopping ads may go the other way; moral words cancel it
how_to_use: Name the mistake, the problem, the thing gone wrong in the first line; do not decorate with 'love/beautiful/pretty'.
source: Robertson et al., Negativity drives online news consumption, Nature Human Behaviour 7, 2023

rule: Write it simpler: common words, short sentences, spoken style. Ordinary readers pick the simple headline; professional writers do not see the difference.
result: Real clicks: Washington Post r=.055 (7,371 tests), Upworthy r=.022 (22,664 tests) — tiny. In a lab choice among 10 headlines: simple target chosen by 34.8 % vs its control 15.3 %; complex target by 22.2 % vs control 27.7 % (odds 2.83). Phrases remembered better: d' 1.23 vs 0.80.
measured_by: Shulman, Markowitz, Rogers, Science Advances 2024: RANDOMISED tests at two sites (pre-registered), plus lab N=524 RANDOMISED, and 249 professional writers (no effect). Clicks/choice/memory, not buying. Repeated across two sites; but Gligorić found readability alone null and Banerjee & Urminsky found longer/harder sentences win.
fails: tiny in the field; character count not a factor at WaPo, longer better at Upworthy
how_to_use: Keep the length, replace every rare word. Let an outsider, not a copywriter, read the draft.
source: Shulman, Markowitz, Rogers, Reading dies in complexity, Science Advances 10, 2024
doubt: field size tiny, lab size large — the truth for a client lies nearer the field size

rule: After the click, easy writing is what keeps them: easier words and sentences make about a quarter more readers finish; concrete and familiar words also hold.
result: One standard deviation easier to read: about +25 % chance of finishing. Coefficients per SD: readability .065–.070, simple syntax .051, concreteness .046–.051, familiar words .028 (all p<.001). How it is written matters as much as, sometimes more than, the topic.
measured_by: Berger, Moe, Schweidel, Journal of Marketing 2023: 649,129 reading sessions, over 35,000 articles of 9 publishers, 6,994,372 paragraph decisions. NOT randomised for this part (heavy controls). Reading on, not buying.
fails: no experiment on the ease part; written text only
how_to_use: Landing page and caption: one idea per short sentence, things you can touch, words a 12-year-old knows.
source: Berger, Moe, Schweidel, What Holds Attention?, Journal of Marketing 2023
doubt: observational for processing ease

rule: To keep them reading, leave them uneasy, not sad: worry holds best, anger next, sadness lets go.
result: Only the emotion words changed: 80 % wanted to read on with anxious words, 71 % with angry, 52 % with sad. In 649,129 real sessions anxiety +14 % finishing per SD (β .042), anger β .011, sadness β −.036; surprise holds, disgust loses.
measured_by: Berger, Moe, Schweidel 2023: study 2 RANDOMISED N=278; field data observational. Reading on, not buying.
fails: for the CLICK it is the reverse: sad words +, fear words − (Robertson 2023)
how_to_use: Headline may name a loss; the first sentences must carry an open question that matters to the reader ('worried', 'not sure yet'), and then resolve it.
source: Berger, Moe, Schweidel 2023

rule: Talk concretely to a customer ('that T-shirt in grey', not 'that'): they spend more afterwards.
result: One standard deviation more concrete e-mail reply: spending in the next 90 days $32.73 → $42.80 (+30 %); careful model +$4 (+13 %). Phone calls: satisfaction +9 %. Lab, RANDOMISED: satisfaction and wish to buy 3.73 vs 3.16 (1–7).
measured_by: Packard & Berger (working paper May 2020, JCR 2021): 940 e-mail cases at a Canadian retailer (observational, spending before controlled); lab studies RANDOMISED N=206 and more
fails: not cold adverts; buying part not randomised; works only when the reply is about what the customer asked
how_to_use: DM and comment replies, chat scripts: name the thing, its colour, its size.
source: Packard & Berger, How Concrete Language Shapes Customer Satisfaction, working paper May 2020
doubt: observational purchase data

rule: When the next step is FREE, cut the sentence off: curiosity then works.
result: Wish to read on (1–7): unfinished 4.27 vs finished 3.30 (text, p=.002); wish to watch: 4.78 vs 4.05 (video, p=.049).
measured_by: Mandler et al. 2024, RANDOMISED, studies 3a (N=279), 3b (N=179), 4 (N=400, pre-registered)
fails: intention only, not actual viewing
how_to_use: Free video, free guide, caption 'more' fold: end on an open sentence. Same line on a paid product: close it.
source: Mandler et al. 2024
doubt: stated intention; students

rule: 'Curiosity headline or plain summary?' has no general winner: nine earlier experiments split three lose, two win, four nothing.
result: Across nine reported lab and field experiments 3 negative significant, 2 positive significant, 4 not different from chance.
measured_by: Aubin Le Quéré & Matias 2025, Table 1 (Scacco & Muddiman 2019 N=2,057; Janét 2020 N=900; Molina 2021 N=150; Menon & Soman 2002 N=131 …)
how_to_use: Never sell a client 'curiosity always wins'; test one curious and one plain version.
source: Aubin Le Quéré & Matias 2025

rule: Clickbait tricks do not out-pull a plain headline when the story is the same — they make no difference at all.
result: Same story, eight headline styles, one per person: no difference in clicking (χ²=4.42, p=.73), sharing (p=.89), curiosity (p=.30) or trust (p=.22). With different stories (study 1) plain ones won: 84 clicks vs question 59, 'must/should' 55, negative superlative 62, 'this' 71, list 77, 'what/why' 74 (odds 2.22 vs modals, 1.97 vs questions).
measured_by: Molina et al., CHI 2021: study 1 RANDOMISED within person N=149 but topics differed; study 2 RANDOMISED N=249 same story. Intent-click in a survey, not live; no sales.
fails: on 371 real Facebook headlines 'this', lists and wh-words got MORE engagement than plain ones — with the topic not held fixed
how_to_use: Do not pay for tricks; the trick-free summary is a fair starting arm in every test.
source: Molina et al., Does Clickbait Actually Attract More Clicks?, CHI 2021
doubt: N≈31 per headline in study 2: a small effect could not be seen

rule: In shop e-mail subject lines the winning move is 'YOU have got it': 'You're getting…', 'You've been selected…', 'We're treating you'. Emojis, cute seasonal puns and bare numbers are what the winner takes out.
result: Features most added by the +32 % model: being chosen/choice ('You've been selected…'), 'we' announcing, the word 'you'. Most removed: social-media phrasing, emojis, numbers and percentages as the lead.
measured_by: Same study, Appendix E, descriptive comparison of 36 field pairs; not a test of each feature
fails: on news headlines 'you' is neutral/negative and digits positive — the channel decides; 'You've been selected' must be TRUE for every receiver (else it is deception)
how_to_use: Offer mail: hand it over in the second person, then the offer ('You're getting 20 % off every oak table').
source: Angelopoulos, Lee, Misra, Causal Alignment, App. E
doubt: authors say: descriptive, does not show which feature caused it

rule: Longer headlines in plain words win on average; a slogan is usually too thin.
result: Length β +0.040 per SD (the largest wording effect in the paper, 2.6 times the negativity effect); complexity −0.004. Gligorić: the longer of two wins about 52 in 100 (β .07) [mine].
measured_by: Robertson et al. 2023 and Gligorić et al. 2023, both RANDOMISED Upworthy tests; average length 15 words
fails: e-mail subjects and bodies go short; Hagar's Chartbeat data disagrees on length (Gligorić discussion)
how_to_use: Spend 12–18 easy words to give the situation; do not cut to a slogan.
source: Robertson et al. 2023

rule: Words that point forward without naming ('this', 'he'), words of seeing ('watch', 'look'), past tense, numbers and concrete nouns raise clicks; how-to/question words, present tense, happy words and touch/taste words lower them.
result: Bonferroni-safe signs (per SD, on mean CTR 1.6 %): forward reference +0.00048, visual +0.00058, long/harder sentences +0.00048, numbers +0.00032, emotional intensity +0.00045, deliberation +; information-seeking (question/how-to) −0.00054, present vs past −0.00050, other senses −0.00018, positive emotion −0.00049. Each is about 1–4 % of clicks [mine].
measured_by: Banerjee & Urminsky draft 2021: 3,346 RANDOMISED tests; clicks only
fails: draft; 'harder to read wins' contradicts Robertson (complexity lowers) — the measure mixes length with difficulty
how_to_use: 'Watch what she did with one board' beats 'How to fix a board'.
source: Banerjee & Urminsky draft 2021
doubt: exploratory draft

rule: 'A' beats 'the': introduce something as new ('a woman', 'an idea') instead of as already known.
result: a/an: logit +0.12 (p=8e-9), about 53 wins in 100 pairs [mine]; 'the': +0.03, not supported.
measured_by: Gligorić et al. 2023, 24,333 randomised pairs; Tan, Lee & Pang 2014 found the same on paired tweets (see that row); Gligorić's own pilot did not reach significance.
fails: small; not tested on sales
how_to_use: Open with 'A carpenter…', not 'The carpenter…'.
source: Gligorić et al., PLOS ONE 2023
doubt: very small

rule: Preachy, moral words cost clicks, and they cancel the gain of a negative word.
result: Share of moral words: β −0.024 (p<.001), interaction with negative −0.007, with positive −0.006.
measured_by: Robertson et al. 2023, 53,699 headlines, RANDOMISED tests
holds: Upworthy — a site that lived on moral causes
fails: not tested elsewhere
how_to_use: Show what happened; leave 'should, duty, justice, right' out of the first line.
source: Robertson et al. 2023

rule: It is the SAD word that gets clicked, not the frightening or angry one: fear words lose clicks, anger words do nothing.
result: Per one standard deviation: sadness +0.7 % odds of a click; fear −0.7 %; joy −0.9 %; anger no effect (inconclusive). The authors had predicted fear and anger would win.
measured_by: Robertson et al. 2023, 39,897 headlines with emotion words, RANDOMISED tests
fails: sharing (Berger & Milkman) and finishing (Berger, Moe, Schweidel) go the other way for anger and anxiety — click, finish and share are three different jobs
how_to_use: Do not open with a scare; open with a loss or a disappointment a person feels.
source: Robertson et al. 2023
doubt: tiny effects; word-list measurement agrees only weakly with human judgement (r 0.22–0.30)

rule: Mentions of money and bossy words ('power', 'lead', 'win over') lower clicks in stories.
result: Money words β −0.00021 (p<.001), dominance words β −0.00029 (p<.001), about −1.3 % and −1.8 % per SD [mine].
measured_by: Banerjee & Urminsky draft 2021, 3,346 RANDOMISED tests; repeated by the first-round measurement on the full archive (money −7.3 %)
fails: shop ads: a price can be the hook (Anyword, Meta ads)
how_to_use: Keep price out of the story hook; keep it in the offer ad.
source: Banerjee & Urminsky draft 2021
doubt: exploratory draft

rule: The textbooks guess the direction wrong more often than right: of 21 clear predictions from psychology, only 7 came out as predicted.
result: 21 constructs with a clear prediction: 7 in the predicted direction (5 significant), 14 the opposite way (8 significant). The published abstract says the same in words.
measured_by: Banerjee & Urminsky, 3,346 RANDOMISED tests (draft); conclusion kept in the published 2024 abstract
how_to_use: Trust a result on this kind of audience over any theory; test.
source: Banerjee & Urminsky draft 2021; abstract Marketing Science 2024

rule: Even randomised headline tests do not say WHICH word did it: the two lines differ in about 18 words, and changing the statistical method changes the sign.
result: Pairs differ on average by 17.67 words; correlation between the new causal model and the plain test difference is 0.11; every one of 43 word groups had at least 15 confounding word groups. When only one word changes, both agree.
measured_by: Lemaire, Yin, Netzer: 1,558 Upworthy tests, 7,498 headlines, 128,390 pairs
how_to_use: To learn a rule for a client, change ONE thing between two arms; to find a winner, change everything.
source: Lemaire, Yin, Netzer, Words That Matter
doubt: working paper; its own per-word results disagree with randomised one-feature results, so they are not copied here

rule: An AI writer that is told WHY past winners won beats both the human headline and an AI that only copies winners.
result: Of 1,420 choices among three versions: AI with learned reasons 38.0 %, AI trained only on winners 31.5 %, the original human headline 30.5 % (p<.001); it was the favourite on 44 of 100 articles against 29 for the human line. In shop words: for every 100 people choosing the human line, about 125 choose this one [mine].
measured_by: Wang, Sudhir, Zhou (Yale, 2025 working paper): randomised order, 142 US Prolific people, 100 articles; stated choice in a survey, not live clicks; trained on 23,437 A/B-tested Upworthy headlines, 4,502 articles
holds: headline writing with a small (3B) model; biggest gain when only 10–25 % of the data is available
fails: the plain winner-trained AI only equalled the humans; no purchases; not repeated
how_to_use: Give the writer 5–10 validated reasons (with pairs) in the brief, not only a pile of winners.
source: Wang, Sudhir, Zhou, Why it Works: Can LLM Hypotheses Improve AI Generated Marketing Content?, Yale working paper, 2025
doubt: survey choice, 100 articles; main scores come from a model judging a model

rule: An AI trained only on clicks turns into a clickbait machine, and today's readers notice.
result: After click-only training 'shocking' rose from 0.7 % to 43.7 % of headlines and 'this is' from 2 % to 56 %; yet people picked those headlines no more than the human ones (31.5 vs 30.5 %).
measured_by: Wang, Sudhir, Zhou 2025; 142 people, 1,420 choices
how_to_use: Cap any scorer: no phrase may exceed its natural share in the drafts.
source: Wang, Sudhir, Zhou 2025

rule: Inside 2013–15 tests certain phrases really did win: 'shocking' 72.5 % of its duels, 'what happens' 67.4 %, 'truth' 65.9 %, 'first' 65.3 %, 'never' 65.1 %, 'dark' 61.4 %, 'this is' 60.2 %, 'one thing' 59.5 %.
measured_by: Wang, Sudhir, Zhou 2025, pairs from Upworthy RANDOMISED tests with a significant winner; the CTR uplift is a raw comparison across articles, the win rate is within pairs
fails: 2025 survey readers found this style 'clickbait' and did not prefer it
how_to_use: 'Never', 'first', 'what happens' survive as honest words; 'shocking' only if it is.
source: Wang, Sudhir, Zhou 2025, Table 3
doubt: raw CTR comparison confounded by article; only pairs with a clear winner; the table columns were aligned by me from the PDF text

rule: The big open archive of headline tests is trustworthy only after dropping one window: 25 June 2013 – 10 January 2014.
result: 22 % of the 32,487 tests are suspect (a cache served one arm at a time); seven research teams re-ran without them and no finding changed.
measured_by: Matias et al., Upworthy Research Archive update 2024
fails: tests are 'intent-to-treat': the headline sat low on a page and many never saw it; no sales data
how_to_use: Drop that window before training any scorer; do not read CTR levels as ad CTR.
source: Matias, Upworthy Archive update, 2024

rule: Do not ask an AI to play ten different customers and average them; asked once as a plain reader it picks the winner more often.
result: 188 tests with one clear winner: plain reader GPT-4.1 61.7 % vs persona panel 42.0 %; Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite 54.8 % vs 39.1 %. (Random about 30 % on the looser set.) It caught 65 % / 59 % of the possible click gain vs 47 % / 46 %.
measured_by: Maiorano, arXiv 2609.25010v2, Nov 2026, one author; outcomes from RANDOMISED Upworthy tests; cohort picked for clear winners
holds: also after dropping the bad-randomisation window (+11 and +22 points)
fails: on Reddit titles the panel won (40.3 vs 30.2 %); Upworthy text may be in the models' training
how_to_use: For a quick sieve: thirty plain 'how likely to click' scores per line, averaged; then a live test.
source: Maiorano, Do Synthetic Personas Predict Real Audience Response?, 2026
doubt: exploratory, only clear-cut tests; author says no universal claim

rule: People pass on what stirs them up (awe, anger, worry, amusement) and what is useful; they keep sad things to themselves.
result: NYT most-e-mailed list, per one standard deviation: anger +34 %, awe +30 %, practical use +30 %, interest +25 %, anxiety +21 %, emotional words +18 %, surprise +14 %, positivity +13 %, sadness −16 %; an hour-long top spot on the home page +20 %. Lab, wish to share (1–7): funny ad 3.97 vs 2.92; 'United Smashes Guitars' story 5.71 vs 'Dents' 3.37; very sad 2.39 vs less sad 3.80.
measured_by: Berger & Milkman, JMR 2012: 6,956 articles (2,566 hand-coded), observational with controls; three RANDOMISED lab studies N=49, 45, 47. Sharing, not buying. Anger/anxiety part repeated for finishing (Berger, Moe, Schweidel), NOT for clicking (Robertson: fear −, anger 0, sadness +).
fails: blogs: useful content was shared less; clicks behave differently
how_to_use: Choose by goal. To travel: useful + awe/amusement. To be clicked: a loss or a surprise. To be read through: unease.
source: Berger & Milkman, What Makes Online Content Viral?, JMR 2012
doubt: main study observational; lab samples under 50

rule: On the happy side: excitement and hope hold, calm contentment does not.
result: Wish to read on (1–7): excitement 4.44, hope 4.15, contentment 3.57.
measured_by: Berger, Moe, Schweidel 2023, study 3, pre-registered RANDOMISED, N=248; the feeling was induced before reading the same neutral text
fails: feeling came from a separate task, not from the copy
how_to_use: 'Soon', 'what if it works' beats 'relax, all is well'.
source: Berger, Moe, Schweidel 2023

rule: A story stopped in the middle is picked up again, not remembered better: 'they cannot get it out of their head' is a myth.
result: Memory for unfinished vs finished tasks: ratio 0.99 (no advantage); unfinished tasks are resumed in 67.06 % of cases on average.
measured_by: Ghibellini & Meier, HSS Communications 2025, meta-analysis of the Zeigarnik and Ovsiankina studies; lab tasks, not adverts
fails: no advert, no sale; heterogeneous methods
how_to_use: Make the viewer start something ('tap the first drawer'), stop, offer to finish. Strike 'Zeigarnik effect' from every brief.
source: Ghibellini & Meier, Interruption, recall and resumption, HSS Communications 12:962, 2025

rule: Serial stories: a stronger cliff-hanger makes the impatient buyers pay — and they are nearly two-thirds of all sales; the patient ones do not care.
result: Stronger cliff-hanger or faster pace raised the chance that impatient readers paid rather than waited; no difference for patient readers. Adding 'wait for free' raised impatient readers' spend by 36 % and halved the patient readers' spend.
measured_by: Lee, Sudhir, Wang (Yale / UT Dallas): 15 months, over 10,000 novels, over 1 million users; behavioural model and SIMULATION, not randomised
fails: the 36 % is a model simulation; article about the paper read, not the paper
how_to_use: Series sold part by part: strongest open ending at the paid step — for people already reading; the cold paid ad still needs a finished sentence (Mandler).
source: Yale Insights, 4 Nov 2026, on Lee, Sudhir, Wang, SSRN 6331041

rule: Want it passed on? Ask plainly, say more, put in a digit and a feeling, talk about a third person, and sound like your own followers; do not tag people.
result: In 11,404 pairs (same author, same link, within 12 hours): 'rt/retweet/please/spread' up (p<1e-20 for rt/retweet), longer up, verbs and nouns up, proper nouns and numbers up, positive AND negative words up (both together too), a/an up, he/she and they up, easier reading up; @-mention down; 'the', 'I', 'we', 'you' nothing. Best word list: rt, retweet, [num], breaking, win, never, people, need, official. Worst: colon, [at], icymi, also, comments, half, question mark, earlier, thanks, sorry.
measured_by: Tan, Lee, Pang, ACL 2014; natural experiment, pairs with a big difference in retweets, Bonferroni over 39 tests; 1,770 fresh pairs held out (65.6 % right). NOT randomised (one tweet came first). Humans: 61.3 % right, majority of 39 people 73 %.
fails: authors themselves add @ and 'you' although they do not help; platform has changed; shares, not sales
how_to_use: Caption meant to travel: one open request ('send this to the friend who…'), a number, a name, no tags.
source: Tan, Lee, Pang, The effect of wording on message propagation, ACL 2014
doubt: not randomised; arrows in the tables partly lost in the text copy, read from the running text

rule: A crowd guesses better than one person: one judge was right 61 times in 100, the majority of 39 was right 73 times.
result: Average of 106 people 61.3 %; majority vote 73 %; above 90 % when at least 80 % agree (under a third of the pairs).
measured_by: Tan, Lee, Pang 2014, 100 tweet pairs, 39 judgments each
holds: pairs chosen for a big difference
fails: on Upworthy pairs single judges were at 50 %
how_to_use: Show 5 drafts to 30–40 strangers; keep only those where 8 of 10 agree; test the rest live.
source: Tan, Lee, Pang, ACL 2014

rule: On a company's own Facebook page: feeling first, then the product. Price and discount posts alone get the least reaction; feeling PLUS facts beats either alone.
result: Asking a question: comments ×1.69 but fewer likes; a blank to fill in: comments ×3 (+200 %), fewer likes; asking for likes raises both; asking for comments raises comments, lowers likes; price and deal words lowest; hard words lower both; shorter slightly better; links worse; holiday mentions lower comments.
measured_by: Lee, Hosanagar, Nair (Management Science 2018, working paper 2014 read): 106,316 messages, 782 firms, Sept 2011–July 2012, corrected for Facebook's own ranking. NOT randomised; likes and comments, not sales (authors say so).
holds: organic brand pages; differs by industry (consumer products gain comments from deals; celebrities gain from price and product)
fails: old Facebook; 'deal' does help comments for consumer products
how_to_use: Organic post: open with a feeling or a person, add one product fact. For comments use a blank, not a question.
source: Lee, Hosanagar, Nair, Effect of Social Media Marketing Content on Consumer Engagement, working paper Oct 2014
doubt: observational; see the correlation warning row; url is the institute, file was on disk; the address is the institute that hosted the working paper, not reopened

rule: On Facebook, headline words should be short and the stock clickbait phrases left out; the text above the link may be long.
result: Headline: each extra letter of average word length −37.4 % (raw coefficient; ×0.69) shares; stock phrases ('will blow your mind', 'best') ×0.77 reactions, ×0.74 shares, ×0.79 comments; question mark ×0.67 shares; unusual punctuation ('...', '!!!') ×1.73 reactions, ×2.43 shares. Post text: doubling the words ×1.18 shares; stock words 'video/photo/reason' ×1.40 reactions; a question ×0.79 reactions.
measured_by: Jung, Stieglitz et al., PLOS ONE 2022: 4,410 Facebook posts of 10 US/UK newspapers, one week of Nov–Dec 2017. NOT randomised; likes/shares/comments, no clicks, no sales.
fails: questions did not bring comments either (n.s.), against the usual advice
how_to_use: Short words in the headline; say more in the post text; do not ask a question to fish for comments.
source: Jung et al., Click me…!, PLOS ONE 17(6) e0266743, 2022
doubt: observational; the authors report raw coefficients as percentages (0.55 → '55 %', the true ratio is ×1.73); their practical advice (4) contradicts their own table

rule: Four 'clickbait detectors' agree with each other on fewer than half the headlines: the label is in the eye of the beholder.
result: All four agree on 47.17 % of 371 headlines, though each claims high accuracy.
measured_by: Molina et al. 2021, study 3 (real Facebook counts, not randomised)
how_to_use: Never gate a client's copy on one 'clickbait score'.
source: Molina et al., CHI 2021

rule: Tricky or oversized type for the number does not help: it makes people less willing to read, though they remember the number a little better.
result: Font type lowered likelihood to read in general (F=14.2, p<.001) and did not change the digit effect (p=.707); memory for numbers d' 0.26 (hard font) and 0.23 (large) vs 0.16 (regular).
measured_by: Peters et al. 2026, RANDOMISED lab experiment N=765; intent and memory, not buying
fails: a large font was one size only (39 vs 25)
how_to_use: Set the number in the same clean type as the rest.
source: Peters et al. 2026
doubt: stated intent

rule: A headline style wears out: the same trick brings fewer clicks every year.
result: Platform age β −0.309 per SD (p<.001): tests late in Upworthy's life got clearly fewer clicks than early ones.
measured_by: Robertson et al. 2023, 12,448 tests 2013-15. NOT randomised for time (observational over the site's life)
fails: audience growth and Facebook changes are mixed in
how_to_use: Retire a hook pattern when its own results sink; keep many kinds in rotation.
source: Robertson et al. 2023
doubt: time is confounded

rule: 'You' as the one something is done FOR ('I made this for you') is liked; 'you' as the one who does something ('you know how…') is not the lever.
result: Songs, download charts: more 'you' → higher rank (b=.19, p<.001); object 'you' b=.36–.45 (p≈.003), subject 'you' not significant with controls. RANDOMISED lyrics: liking 4.38 ('you') vs 3.68 (he/she) vs 3.93 (none) N=309; 4.01 vs 3.61 vs 3.67 N=1,600 pre-registered, five songs. It works by making people think of someone in their own life.
measured_by: Packard & Berger, Psychological Science 2020: 4,200 chart positions of paid downloads (observational) + two RANDOMISED lab studies on liking
fails: not advertising; on headlines 'you' is null (Gligorić) or negative (Banerjee & Urminsky)
how_to_use: Emotional brand film: say 'for you / to you / of you' so the viewer thinks of her own person.
source: Packard & Berger, Thinking of You, Psychological Science 2020
doubt: field part observational; lab is liking of lyrics

rule: AI-made adverts were preferred to human ones when built on authority or 'others do it'; written to a personality type they only drew level.
result: 59.1 % vs 40.9 % preference (p<.001); authority 63.0 %, consensus 62.5 %; personality-matched 51.1 vs 48.9 % (no difference). Knowing it is AI costs 21.2 points and it still wins.
measured_by: Meguellati et al. 2025: RANDOMISED lab, N=800 and N=400; forced choice, not clicks or buying
fails: stated preference; human ads not from top agencies
how_to_use: Let AI draft the proof-based arms (expert, number of users); spend the human hour elsewhere.
source: Meguellati et al., LLM-Generated Ads, arXiv 2512.03373, Dec 2025
doubt: preference only

rule: Asking for help: say 'thank you' before they give. Requests that thanked in advance were funded more often.
result: DonorsChoose classroom requests 2013, chance of full funding: pre-thanking +6.9 points (causal text model), +3.0 (raw), +1.2 and +0.75 (other models) — same sign everywhere. 'You' words +3.4 points in the causal model, +0.7 raw, about −0.2 in the other two.
measured_by: Lemaire, Yin, Netzer (working paper, 2025): observational donation requests, text-confounder model; NOT randomised; outcome = request fully funded (money given)
holds: charity requests; earlier randomised evidence on restaurant bills (Rind & Bordia 1995) cited
fails: the size depends on the model used; 'you' result flips with the method
how_to_use: Fund-raising or favour-asking opening: start with thanks, then the need.
source: Lemaire, Yin, Netzer, Words That Matter, working paper
doubt: observational; size depends on the model; table columns read in print order from the PDF text

rule: The one strong test FOR questions: on a small-ads site 'Is this your new iPhone4?' pulled far more readers than 'For sale: Black iPhone4 16GB' — but for a washing machine the question lost.
result: Second-hand ads: question to the reader +257 % clicks on average, plain question +137 %, rhetorical +103 %; washing machine −20 to −29 %. Twitter science posts: +150 % / +175 %.
measured_by: Lai & Farbrot, Social Influence 2013/14 (Norway): four fake ads rotated over four weeks on finn.no (3,256 clicks in all); Twitter, question always posted one hour AFTER the statement. Not properly randomised by person; tiny number of items.
holds: fun, wanted goods on a small-ads list
fails: all later large tests (Upworthy 22,743 tests, Ushno −13.5 %, Fang & Wheeler) say the reverse; necessity goods lost
how_to_use: Only as one arm in a marketplace title test for a desired item; never as the rule.
source: Lai & Farbrot, What makes you click?, Social Influence 9(4), 2014
doubt: extract only; fictitious sellers' ads; few items

rule: On TikTok the choice of single words in the spoken opener explains almost nothing; a stronger feeling in it goes with more views, not with more likes or comments.
result: 4,983 hooks: correlation with views 0.02 (p=.17), likes 0.014, comments 0.003. Hooks above the median of views had a higher emotional score (AFINN 1.11 vs 0.81, p<.001; Syuzhet 0.33 vs 0.26, p=.001; third tool no difference); likes and comments no difference.
measured_by: Nastišin et al., Marketing and Management of Innovations 2025; scraped English TikTok transcripts 2020-22. NOT randomised, no account control, no watch time, no sales.
fails: two of three sentiment tools only; 'POV' advice rests on word clouds, not a test
how_to_use: Do not sell a magic-word list for TikTok; write the feeling of the first second clearly.
source: Nastišin et al., A Lexical and Sentiment Analysis of TikTok Hooks, MMI 16(4), 2025
doubt: observational; no control for account size

rule: On TikTok brand hooks, how-to openings got the lowest like rate; urgency, 'don't' and 'you' the highest; the topic matters more than any wording, and under 8 words goes with more likes.
result: Mean like rate: urgency 0.041, 'don't' 0.041, 'you' 0.039, question 0.036, how-to/number first 0.029. Under 8 words about 0.050, over 34 words about 0.028. Emotional vs informational hooks: no difference (p=.13). Random forest: category first, then length, then urgency.
measured_by: Mishra, OSF preprint, Aug 2025: 46,605 hooks of over 1,950 consumer-app brand accounts 2019–25, likes per view. NOT randomised, no account control, not peer reviewed.
fails: like rate is not watch time or sales; the paper's text says curiosity beats 'you' while its own numbers show 'you' (0.039) above questions (0.036)
how_to_use: Idea for a test only: short + a 'don't' line.
source: Mishra, The Science of the First Three Seconds, OSF rj2mz, 2025
doubt: observational; internal contradiction; one author

rule: Stories that jump quickly from one thing to the next are liked more on screen; episodes that try to cover too much ground are liked less; papers are the reverse.
result: One standard deviation faster: film rating +0.048, TV episode +0.072 on a 10-point scale; TV volume negative; academic papers: faster −12 % citations, more ground +10 %, circling back +7 %.
measured_by: Toubia, Berger, Eliashberg, PNAS 2021: 4,118 films, 12,336 TV episodes, 29,300 papers; observational with topic controls. Ratings, not attention or sales.
fails: tiny effect; no adverts; correlation warning applies
how_to_use: Video: move fast between scenes but stay on one subject; text that must convince may circle back.
source: Toubia, Berger, Eliashberg, How quantifying the shape of stories predicts their success, PNAS 118(26), 2021
doubt: observational, small

rule: The longer line is becoming the market's habit: headlines grew by about a quarter word a year for 20 years, with more verbs, pronouns and full sentences.
result: About 40 million headlines, 2000–2020s: longer (+~0.25 word per year), more wh-words, verbs, pronouns, negativity; fewer noun-phrase titles; same trend in quality and tabloid press.
measured_by: Nickl, Moussaïd, Lorenz-Spreen 2025. NOT randomised, no outcome at all — only what publishers write.
fails: does not prove it wins; Kuiken 2017 (cited) found longer rewrites did not change clicks
how_to_use: Background only: a full sentence with a verb is the normal form; a two-word label is out of date.
source: Nickl et al., The evolution of online news headlines, HSS Communications 12:364, 2025
doubt: prevalence is not success

rule: An entertaining video sells only when the exciting part of the picture IS the product; being entertaining and showing the product at different moments does nothing.
result: PE score (how engaging the pixels are where the product stands) is the only significant predictor of sales lift, p<0.01 alone, p<0.001 with all controls; it alone explains 3% of the variance in sales lift (R2 0.03; 0.06 with engagement and product scores; XGBoost 0.47, 0.42 cross-validated). Overall engagement, amount of product on screen, and both-but-apart: all not significant.
measured_by: Yang, Zhang & Zhang, published version Marketing Science 2025: difference-in-differences, 259 treated products (2,426 controls), Taobao revenue, Douyin influencer ads 2019
holds: Cheap, impulsive, hedonic goods on Douyin (working paper Table 5: significant only there); food and make-up are the main categories
fails: Not significant for deliberate, utilitarian or dear products (working paper); not randomised; picture only, sound and words are partialled out; not an opening-seconds measure
how_to_use: Find the striking moment first, then rebuild it so it cannot be shown without the product being the thing that moves (the blender shreds the phone). Do not buy a 'funny first half, product second half' script.
source: Yang, Zhang & Zhang, Engagement That Sells, Marketing Science 44(2):247-267, 2025 (published); checked against the 2022 working paper
doubt: 3% of variance is small: as a rule of construction worth keeping, as a forecast of one client's sales it is not. Observational (posting time). The working paper's negative effect of more product time (p<0.05) vanished in the published version.

rule: The average paid creator video lifts sales by nothing you can distinguish from zero, and followers, price of the creator and likes do not tell you which will.
result: Average lift 2,017 RMB ($292), p=0.50, while the creator charged 19,530 RMB ($2,826) per video on average; correlation of sales change with likes -0.0075 (p=0.90), comments -0.02 (p=0.74), shares -0.0074 (p=0.91); followers and price per video not significant.
measured_by: Yang, Zhang & Zhang 2025, 259 treated products, difference-in-differences
holds: Douyin influencer ads 2019 with Taobao sales
fails: One-video products only; sales imputed from 30-day totals
how_to_use: Never report likes or shares to a client as evidence of sales; judge a creator video by orders, and expect most to do nothing, so test many and keep the winner.
source: Yang, Zhang & Zhang, Marketing Science 44(2), 2025
doubt: Wide spread (SD 47,530 RMB): some ads lift a lot, some lower.

rule: In short videos people, happy or sad faces and energetic or novel doing hold the eye; slow, everyday doing and fearful or surprised faces lose it.
result: Objects in high-engagement pixels 9,916 vs low 4,780, humans the most frequent; happiness and sadness positive, fear and surprise negative; 112 activities positive (salsa, side kick, climbing), 40 negative (shearing sheep, reading books, garbage collecting)
measured_by: Yang, Zhang & Zhang 2025, saliency map trained on shares of 16,951 ads, applied to 2,685 videos; survey of 101 students confirms 'novel, interesting, funny'
fails: Engagement here = shares, and shares did not predict sales; correlational, exploratory, called 'preliminary' by the authors
how_to_use: Use as raw material only: take a moving person and a novel action, and make the product the tool of that action.
source: Yang, Zhang & Zhang, Marketing Science 44(2), 2025
doubt: Not money; do not stake money on it alone.

rule: The eye arrives after the first second: attention to a short video rises steeply, peaks by second 6 and then slopes down, while advertisers spread the product evenly and waste the peak.
result: Engagement score 0.175 at second 1, 0.320 at second 6, 0.318 at 11, 0.295 at 16, 0.240 at 56; product score flat at 0.10-0.11 throughout; overlap of engagement and product maps 0.46
measured_by: Yang, Zhang & Zhang 2025, 2,685 videos, model-inferred
fails: Authors: cannot conclude the product should be placed where average engagement peaks, videos differ widely
how_to_use: Let the product do its strongest thing between seconds 2 and 10, not in the last frame.
source: Yang, Zhang & Zhang, Marketing Science 44(2), 2025, Figure 2
doubt: Figure numbers were read from a converted chart; model-inferred attention, not measured.

rule: A creator shows the product in the striking spot when it is his own product; when he is paid by someone else he keeps the spot for his face.
result: PE score 35% higher (p<0.001) in 77 ads for the creator's own products (28% in the working paper); experience makes no difference
measured_by: Yang, Zhang & Zhang 2025, 77 vs 2,685 videos, regression with controls
fails: 77 videos, not randomised
how_to_use: Give the creator a share of sales or write into the brief exactly which second the product must be the thing that moves.
source: Yang, Zhang & Zhang, Marketing Science 44(2), 2025

rule: The kind of first three seconds that goes with sales differs by trade: make-the-viewer-take-part openings in online shops, showing the product/demonstration in health, good-looking pictures then humour in packaged goods, beauty of the car then realism in cars, celebrity and humour in entertainment.
result: Top topic by importance: e-commerce 'Interactive content', healthcare 'Demo / product', CPG 'Visual appeals' then 'Humor', automobile 'Visual appeals' then 'Realism', entertainment 'Entertainment' then 'Endorsement / celebrity'. R2 of conversions per investment 0.21/0.33/0.50/0.66/0.25 - but this is hook features PLUS gender, age, advertiser size, zip code and other targeting, never the hook alone.
measured_by: Zhang (Univ. Maryland) with Zhang, Hill & Awadelkarim (Meta), arXiv 2602.22299, Feb 2026; Meta ads: e-commerce 100-150k videos, CPG 75-100k, healthcare 25-50k, auto 10-25k, entertainment 10-25k; gradient-boosted trees, correlational
holds: Meta ads above a spend minimum; conversions per investment over the first 56 days
fails: No randomisation; only importance ranks are printed, no size of gain for any hook type; a crude pixel-average predictor beat it in healthcare (R2 0.42 vs 0.33) and ViViT beat it in entertainment; only the e-commerce curve is shown as going up
how_to_use: Use as an order of testing per sector, not as a formula: shop = a choice or game first; clinic = the procedure or product first; food/household = the best-looking shot first.
source: Zhang, Zhang, Hill & Awadelkarim, Decoding the Hook, arXiv 2602.22299, 2026
doubt: The first round wrote 'the first 3 seconds matter for conversions': the paper does not isolate that. No client money on the rank alone. The authors' own 'top-performing' showcase gives no numbers.

rule: The sound of the first three seconds (how loud, how strong, how high the voice goes) is among what goes with sales, and there is a best range, not 'louder is better'.
result: Top acoustic features: e-commerce dB, power, maximum pitch; healthcare power, peak, shimmer; CPG power, peak, ddp; optimal range for dB and maximum pitch, threshold for power. No numbers printed for the range.
measured_by: Zhang et al. (Meta) 2026, partial dependence on 100-150k e-commerce videos; 87-95% of videos have audio
fails: Correlational, range not published
how_to_use: Test two sound levels of the same opening; do not start in silence or at a shout by default.
source: Zhang, Zhang, Hill & Awadelkarim, Decoding the Hook, arXiv 2602.22299, 2026
doubt: No effect size; hypothesis to test.

rule: People stay with an ad while their joy is RISING; a steady smile keeps the eye but a change upward keeps the person, and a drop costs less than a rise gains - so give a small laugh, let it fall, give another.
result: Emotions carry 72% of the model's explained zapping (58% from changes in joy alone; model R2 63%). Joy velocity -1.818 vs joy level -.398 vs surprise level -.164 (standardised probit). Modelled retention gain: peak-valley-peak best; best real ad (Bud Light 'Swear jar') about 50% better retention than a steadily rising line.
measured_by: Teixeira, Wedel & Pieters, JMR 2012; laboratory, 58 paid students/staff (50 in the analysis), 28 video ads, 145,000 quarter-second frames, facial coding + eye tracking + real zapping by space bar; first 30 s only
holds: Humorous TV-style ads shown as post-rolls to students, average zapping 48%
fails: Ads not randomly chosen, emotions not randomised inside the ad, no purchase or intent measured
how_to_use: Write three small joyful turns in 20-30 s instead of one joke at the end; make each turn higher than the last.
source: Teixeira, Wedel & Pieters, Emotion-Induced Engagement in Internet Video Advertisements, JMR 2012
doubt: The 72% is a share of EXPLAINED zapping, not of all zapping; watching only, students, 2010 desk setting. Not client money on its own.

rule: Surprise pulls every eye to one spot, and it does so best early; later surprise saves fewer viewers.
result: Surprise level effect on attention dispersion -.105 vs joy -.032 (three times), largest of 14 predictors (29%); early surprise reduces zapping more than late; reaction to it falls out in 500-750 ms
measured_by: Teixeira, Wedel & Pieters 2012, same experiment (N 50 people x 28 ads)
fails: Authors: early advantage may be selection, because bored people have already left; direct effect of surprise on staying is far smaller than joy's
how_to_use: Use surprise in second 0-2 only to point the eye at the product, then switch to joy; never rely on surprise to carry the video.
source: Teixeira, Wedel & Pieters, JMR 2012
doubt: Selection not separated.

rule: Keeping the payoff for the end loses people: the mystery that stays flat and bursts at the last second is the worst shape of five.
result: Stable-and-peak ('typical for certain mystery advertisements') performs worst on both attention and retention among five emotion shapes; peak-and-stable best for attention, peak-valley-peak best for retention
measured_by: Teixeira, Wedel & Pieters 2012, model simulation from 28 ads, 50 viewers
holds: Skippable ads up to 30 s, model-based
fails: Simulated, not shown to people; tension ads with a question opened early not modelled
how_to_use: Pay something out in the first seconds even when a bigger answer waits.
source: Teixeira, Wedel & Pieters, JMR 2012
doubt: Simulation.

rule: A frame that is too bare or too crowded loses people; a middling amount of things in the picture keeps them.
result: U-shaped effect of visual complexity on zapping: both lower and higher complexity increase zapping relative to medium (coefficient .033 on squared, standardised)
measured_by: Teixeira, Wedel & Pieters 2012, 28 ads, 50 viewers
fails: Small next to emotion (all non-emotion, non-familiarity factors together 10% of explained variation)
how_to_use: One subject plus enough setting to read it; do not open on a blank card or a collage.
source: Teixeira, Wedel & Pieters, JMR 2012

rule: A joke before the viewer knows whose ad it is holds him but does not make him want to buy; the same joke after the brand has been seen does.
result: Smiling after first brand sight: positive and linear on purchase intent (0.698, significant; 0.989 for amount). Smiling before: no positive linear effect (0.312 ns), marginally negative (-0.189 linear-only; squared -0.800). Pure entertainment moves intent by 21% across ads (scale mean 4.4 of 10).
measured_by: Teixeira, Picard & el Kaliouby, Marketing Science 2014; 178 people at home, 82 real TV ads (3,487 views), order randomised, webcam smile coding, skip key, stated purchase intent 0-10; entertainment level NOT randomised
holds: Confectionery, soft drinks, alcohol; first-time views (86.3% of data)
fails: Stated intent, not buying; marginal significance for the 'before' half; known brands; the authors add that ads to make people merely curious (new product) may hold the brand back
how_to_use: Show whose thing it is (product in hand, not a logo card) in the first third, then spend your best laugh; the brand only at the end gave the lowest intent at every level of fun.
source: Teixeira, Picard & el Kaliouby, Why, When, and How Much to Entertain Consumers in Advertisements?, Marketing Science 2014
doubt: Contradicts 'brand late' findings on sharing (Tellis) and on skipping (Teixeira 2010): late brand buys views, early brand buys intent.

rule: More fun always keeps more people to the end, but past a middling amount it makes fewer of them want the product.
result: Viewing rises straight with smiling (0.987); purchase intent is an upside-down U (0.905 linear, -1.014 squared); 23% of ads already too funny for at least some viewers; 40% of people individually show a significant turn-down, 57-64% the shape; most others keep rising
measured_by: Teixeira, Picard & el Kaliouby 2014, 178 people, 82 ads
fails: Intent only; only 7 of 82 ads lie in the top two deciles where intent falls
how_to_use: When watch time goes up after a funnier opening, check orders before scaling it.
source: Teixeira, Picard & el Kaliouby, Marketing Science 2014
doubt: Shape is found in a minority to a small majority of persons.

rule: If you want people to PASS ON the video, keep the brand name to the end: naming it at the start costs about a third of the shares.
