result: Brand early vs at end: -29.88% shares (p=.002) in study 1, -35.60% (p=.002) in study 2; brand here and there -26.51% (p=.008) and -31.61% (p=.010)
measured_by: Tellis, MacInnis, Tirunillai & Zhang, MSI working paper 19-110 of Journal of Marketing 2019; study 1 345 YouTube ads of 109 US brands (from 1,962), study 2 512 ads of 228 brands; real 30-day shares on Facebook, Twitter, Google+, LinkedIn; coders; mixed-effects regression, observational
holds: Big brands' voluntary YouTube ads 2013-2017, replicated
fails: By platform the early-vs-late difference is not significant on any single one (Table A3); not about buying; small firms untested
how_to_use: For an unpaid film meant to travel: person and event first, brand name last (the product itself may be in the story). For a paid selling ad the opposite holds (see Teixeira 2014).
source: Tellis, MacInnis, Tirunillai & Zhang, What Drives Virality, MSI 19-110 / J. Marketing 83(4), 2019
doubt: Not randomised; brands that brand late may make better films. Working paper read, journal page only partly. Read: abstract, method, all results and discussion; theory/literature part skipped.

rule: A video that argues with facts is shared about a fifth to a third less for each step on a six-point scale - unless the product is new or expensive, or the network is LinkedIn.
result: Argument -32.56% (p=.002) and -18.13% (p=.005) shares per step; for a NEW product +27.76% (p=.042) / +28.40% (p=.05) back; for a HIGH-priced one +39.38% (p=.028) / +29.69% (p=.027); LinkedIn no penalty (p=.569). New product as such +57.78% / +25.86%
measured_by: Tellis et al., 345 + 512 YouTube ads, two independent periods and coders
fails: Moderately priced products: helped in study 1, not in study 2
how_to_use: Cheap everyday goods: no arguments in the travelling video. New or dear goods (implants, kitchens, software for firms): open on the new fact.
source: Tellis et al., MSI 19-110 / J. Marketing 2019
doubt: Sharing, not buying; facts are known to lower clicks while raising sales in TV work. Read: abstract, method, all results and discussion; theory/literature part skipped.

rule: Babies and animals, then celebrities, then a film-like little story make a video travel; only babies/animals are cheap and almost nobody uses them.
result: Facebook log-share effects: baby/animal 2.382 (p=.003), celebrity 0.854 (p=.010); baby/animal raises warmth 1.237, inspiration .588, amusement .453; drama raises amusement .54; used in under 3% (baby/animal), 11% (strong drama), 26% (celebrity) of ads. Not significant on LinkedIn.
measured_by: Tellis et al., 345 YouTube ads, study 1 (replicated in sign in study 2)
fails: LinkedIn (.114, .186); baby/animal present in only 13 ads, so the size is shaky; suspense and sex appeal no effect
how_to_use: Give the shop's clip a baby, dog or cat that meets the product; sensible where it fits the trade.
source: Tellis et al., MSI 19-110, Tables 5, 6, A2
doubt: 13 of 345 ads had a baby/animal. Read: abstract, method, all results and discussion; theory/literature part skipped.

rule: Surprise is worth it because it makes people laugh; putting it at the start rather than elsewhere gave no extra shares.
result: Surprise on amusement .183 (p<.001), on inspiration -.13; 'surprise early' vs others not significant on any network (-1.948 p=.222; -0.270 p=.823; -2.219 p=.077; -1.505 p=.166); only 11 of 345 ads had early surprise
measured_by: Tellis et al., study 1, Table A3
fails: Tiny cell (11 ads); direction negative
how_to_use: Do not sell 'surprise in second 1' to a client as proven for sharing; let the surprise resolve the little story.
source: Tellis et al., MSI 19-110, Table 6 and A3
doubt: 11 ads. Read: abstract, method, all results and discussion; theory/literature part skipped.

rule: A film that went truly viral (over a million shares) was followed by a small rise in the firm's share price.
result: Mean abnormal return +1.41% over 30 trading days, 137 events, Z=2.93 (p=.002); sign test p=.04
measured_by: Tellis et al., study 4, event study on 137 viral videos of listed firms
fails: Daily sales were not available; share price is a guess by investors; confounded with launches and other news
how_to_use: Background only: virality is not worthless, but never an argument for a small shop's sales.
source: Tellis et al., MSI 19-110, study 4
doubt: Indirect money. Read: abstract, method, all results and discussion; theory/literature part skipped.

rule: Simple frame, quick change: show one important thing in the middle of the screen, undisturbed for a full second, at the start of the video or right after a cut - the eyes of the audience gather about two thirds of a second after the cut.
result: Per scene: 1 SD more clutter = about 12% less shared gaze; each extra second of scene = about 5% less (431 scenes, p=.003, p<.001). Per frame: +1 SD clutter -26.4% [22.8, 30.1], a cut +40.2% [30.9, 49.6], peak at about 0.66 s; each extra cut gives less when cuts are many
measured_by: Wals, Grewal, Wilms et al., JAMS 2025; 30 Dutch adults (18-59) x 42 government adverts seen twice = 2,520 viewings, eye tracking, forced viewing
holds: 25-30 s public-service films, young and old alike
fails: No skipping, no clicking, no buying; scenes under one second do not exist in the sample; features not randomised; 30 people only
how_to_use: Second 0: product or face alone, centred, 1 s; cut; next single thing. Put the key word 0.7 s after a cut, never on the cut.
source: Wals, Grewal, Wilms et al., The dynamic effects of visual complexity and scene cuts on viewer attention, JAMS 2025
doubt: Gaze alignment, then liking (slope 0.82 [0.03,1.61]) and recognition after 48-72 h (0.88 [0.25,1.52]) only; no money. Read: abstract, method, all results and discussion; theory/literature part skipped.

rule: A close-up of a person pulls the eyes together most; a half-length figure in front of a busy background scatters them.
result: Close-up +18.6% shared gaze [6.14, 31.11] p=.004; medium shot +9.77% [0.36, 19.18] p=.042; medium shot x clutter -17.84 [-28.17,-7.51] p=.001, vs scenes without a person
measured_by: Wals et al., JAMS 2025, exploratory, 431 scenes (55 close-ups, 143 medium, 110 wide, 114 none)
fails: Exploratory; face-first lowered early views in skippable ads elsewhere (Marketing Letters 2026)
how_to_use: If you open on a person, open close; if the room must be seen, take the person out or empty the room.
source: Wals et al., JAMS 2025
doubt: Exploratory, gaze only. Read: abstract, method, all results and discussion; theory/literature part skipped.

rule: The first four seconds tell how often and how long a video will be watched - and what matters is that they feel like a promise of something good and not like something unpleasant.
result: Reward-area brain activity at onset: +0.65 SD views per SD (28% of variance in views per day across 36 videos); unease area -0.54; middle or end of the video did not forecast. What people SAID or CHOSE did not forecast views at all (adj R2 -0.004 and 0.005).
measured_by: Tong, Acikalin, Genevsky, Shiv & Knutson, PNAS 2020; 36 people in fMRI scanner, 36 YouTube videos forecast against their real YouTube views per day and watch share
fails: Unease effect vanishes in rank correlation (rho -0.09, p=.61); no selling videos; YouTube numbers were collected before the scans; classification accuracy 59-69%
how_to_use: Open on a thing people look forward to; do not trust a survey 'would you watch this' - show the first 4 s and measure whether they stay.
source: Tong et al., Brain activity forecasts video engagement in an internet attention market, PNAS 117(12), 2020
doubt: 36 videos, 36 people; views not sales. File named tongpmc.txt in the raw folder is a different paper (schizophrenia) - tongfull.txt is the right one. Read: abstract, method, all results and discussion; theory/literature part skipped.

rule: On long YouTube videos the first 30 seconds carry more of the reaction than the middle or the end, and what is SAID carries more than twice what the picture or the sound does; the title carries most of all.
result: Share of combined-model importance: captions begin vs middle vs end larger in every outcome; text >2x audio or video frames; title the best single predictor; holdout accuracy only 63-72% (binary), multimodal permutation text vs audio p<0.001
measured_by: Rajaram & Manchanda, working paper Apr 2025: 1,620 videos of 33 top US influencers (50 each), likes/comments per view, 25-50 bootstraps
fails: Comments and likes given the view - not watching, not buying; 72% of the associations a normal analysis would report were spurious by their own test
how_to_use: Spend the writing time on title and the first sentences before spending on pictures.
source: Rajaram & Manchanda, Unboxing Engagement in YouTube Influencer Videos, 2025 version
doubt: Engagement only, 33 famous creators; no client money.

rule: Thumbnail picture must show what the title says; but the words ON the thumbnail must not repeat the title.
result: 10,098 videos of 233 creators: picture-title match goes with more views, overlay-text-title match with fewer; preregistered experiment N=996: more picture-title match raised curiosity and choice, more text-title match did not. Sizes not in the abstract.
measured_by: Cho, Sim, Cho & Eom, SSRN 30 Sep 2026, field + preregistered experiment (AI-made thumbnails)
fails: Views and choices, not sales; sizes not printed in abstract
how_to_use: Picture = the thing in the title; overlay = a different fact that opens a gap the video will close.
source: Cho et al., Catchy or Sketchy?, SSRN 7543822, 2026 (abstract)
doubt: Abstract only; working paper.

rule: A seller on live video who shows some fellow-feeling sells more; one who lays it on thick sells less because it looks put on.
result: Inverted U between perceived empathy and purchases in almost 4,000 livestream videos; causal in pre-registered experiments incl. a randomised field experiment with 6,000 customers. No sizes in the abstract.
measured_by: Luo, Berger, Fang & Huang, forthcoming Management Science (SSRN 7530660)
fails: Sizes not read; not about second 1
how_to_use: One honest 'I had that too' sentence, then the product.
source: Luo, Berger, Fang & Huang, When Perceived Empathy Sells (abstract)
doubt: Abstract only.

rule: An excited VOICE sells more on live video, above all for things you must experience and for well-known hosts.
result: Vocal arousal significantly increases sales on Taobao Live; replicated in a controlled experiment with the same words; sizes not in abstract
measured_by: Yao, Ren, Li, Shankar & Xu, SSRN 5657931, 2025: thousands of clips linked to product sales + experiment
fails: Weaker for search goods and small hosts; full paper not downloadable
how_to_use: Keep the face calm (see Bharadwaj) and put the energy into the voice.
source: Yao et al., Selling by Voice (abstract)
doubt: Abstract only.

rule: Let a second (third) voice carry on the same sales message, spoken slowly: people gave more money to products presented by more than one voice.
result: Field: each extra voice went with about $12,795 more pledged (+39%), 118 more backers (+38%), 1.6 points more chance of reaching the goal (+6.5%). Experiments: willing to pay $47.98 (five voices) vs $44.18 (one), p=.021, eta2 .015; purchase likelihood 4.17 vs 3.57 of 7, p=.031, eta2 .025. With a distracted listener $43.40 vs $44.81: no gain; at fast speech the sign turns negative.
measured_by: Chang, Mukherjee & Chattopadhyay, JMR 2023: 11,801 US Kickstarter videos, 3.6 million transactions, $382m (observational, 24 robustness checks); 1,610 ads (rated); two randomised experiments, N 357 and 187, synthetic voices
holds: Product-explaining videos that people chose to watch (Kickstarter page, first exposure)
fails: Fast speech, distracted viewers; not an opening-seconds study; feed scrolling not tested
how_to_use: After the opening line, hand over to a second voice (customer, second presenter) for the next sentence; keep the pace calm. Cheap to test.
source: Chang, Mukherjee & Chattopadhyay, More Voices Persuade, JMR 2023
doubt: The 39% is correlation (richer projects have teams); the randomised part is about +9% stated price, 1.5-2.5% of variance. Worth a cheap test, not a promise. Read: abstract, method, all results and discussion; theory/literature part skipped.

rule: In the first 30 seconds of a creator video, naming a brand sours the comments (mostly in electronics), a moment of music sweetens them, and people or animals on screen get a slightly better like ratio while the packet gets a slightly worse one.
result: Per half second of music alone odds of positive comments +30.6%; 1% more human area +0.4% like-sentiment, animal +1.0%, packaged goods -0.7%; fast talk: no effect; joyful or surprised faces: no effect
measured_by: Rajaram & Manchanda 2025, 1,620 YouTube videos, robust in 80%+ of bootstraps
fails: Not causal; tiny effects for picture; not sales
how_to_use: Let the first 30 s be about the person and the problem; show the packet working rather than standing.
source: Rajaram & Manchanda, 2025
doubt: Sentiment only.

rule: A face in the first five seconds of a skippable YouTube ad goes with FEWER real views when the product is practical; for pleasure products it makes no difference.
result: 0% to 100% of frames with a face: beta -0.6894 on log 7-day qualified views (p<.001) [mine: about half the views]; utilitarian -1.0679 (p=.001) with copula; interaction for hedonic +0.5552 (p=.065); median ad 8,179 views in 7 days
measured_by: Hilton, Malshe & Gretz, Marketing Letters 2026; 3,498 skippable YouTube ads, 685 channels, 23 categories, 2021-23; regression, NOT randomised
fails: Ad budgets, targeting and bids unobserved - 'associational rather than causal'; views depend on money spent; contradicts TikTok Shop sales data (face 1.05x)
how_to_use: For tools, cleaning, insurance-like, home repair on YouTube: open on the object or the result, test the face version beside it.
source: Hilton, Malshe & Gretz, Before the skip option, Marketing Letters 2026
doubt: Budget confound can produce the whole effect; face valence had mean zero.

rule: Play a pleasant, complicated movement in slow motion: people like the clip more, choose the brand more often and say they would pay more; unpleasant or simple movements must stay at normal speed.
result: Brand choice with a real voucher 69.2% vs 30.8% (279 of 403); hotel interest 2.91 vs 2.60 of 5 (p<.001, eta2 .02), relaxation seekers 2.75 vs 2.22, thrill seekers no difference; unpleasant clips liked less in slow motion (b -.265); 514 GIFs in the field: slow motion better (p<.001) only for complex, pleasant content, R2 of whole model .104; willingness to pay for a hotel night $152.70 vs $140.49 (WTP, +9%); pooled Hedges g .38 (p=.003) over five experiments
measured_by: Stuppy, Landwehr & McGraw, JMR 2023; six randomised experiments (199 to 600 US adults each) + 514 GIFs field data; speed varied inside the clip (1.5 s normal then slow)
holds: Pleasant, complex movement; viewers going by gut feeling; relaxing products
fails: Deliberating viewers (gap shrinks), thrill products, simple or ugly movement; slow motion only works beside normal speed
how_to_use: Start at normal speed, drop into slow motion at the beautiful instant (chocolate coating, fabric falling, water closing) - never for complaint or fear scenes.
source: Stuppy, Landwehr & McGraw, slow-motion paper, JMR 2023, DOI 10.1177/00222437231179187
doubt: Online panels, brands unknown, choice of a raffle voucher; brand liking raised by pairing, not by an ad. Effect sizes on interest are small (2% of variance). (outcome label: stated interest/choice, nearest label used)

rule: Most of what a short-video ad brings in arrives somewhere else: exposed people left their phone number eight times more often outside the app than inside it.
result: Lift in leads +112% (0.0820 per 1,000; significant), of which inside the app only 0.0171 per 1,000; cost per lead falls to one fifth (properly measured) or one 25th (as brands usually count) when outside leads are included. For comparison the median lift of 663 Facebook trials is 9%, of 432 Google display trials 8%. Gender, age and city made no difference to the true effect; prior brand home-page visits did.
measured_by: Liang, Chen, Han, Zhang & Chen, Marketing Science 44(5) 2025; preprint read whole: randomised field experiment on Douyin+Toutiao, 84 million users (42m each arm, 8.2% exposed), car brand with all other digital ads switched off, Aug-Nov 2020; conversion = lead form, not a car sold
holds: High-price product, large brand, short videos on ByteDance
fails: One car brand; leads not sales; creative not varied
how_to_use: When two openings are tested for a dentist or a kitchen firm, count calls, forms, walk-ins and brand searches from everywhere; in-app orders alone would pick the wrong winner.
source: Liang et al., Is the Money Spent on Short-Form Video Social Platforms Worth It?, Marketing Science 2025 (preprint of 23 Nov 2023 read)
doubt: The eight-fold is a raw comparison of exposed users; the causal split is 0.0684 vs 0.0171 per 1,000 (four times). Read: abstract, method, all results and discussion; theory/literature part skipped.

rule: In a shop feed, how-to style videos and unevenly cut videos get fewer clicks on the product link, above all from people the algorithm has matched badly.
result: How-to content -2.11 percentage points click probability (p<.01), from -3.0 at low fit to -0.9 (n.s.) at high fit; +0.1 in shot-length unevenness -0.33 points (p<.01)
measured_by: MDPI JTAER 21(10) 381, 2026: 66,244 first-position exposures, 36,542 users, 11,045 videos, household goods, Chinese e-commerce app, July-Aug 2022; regression, not randomised
holds: Household products in a recommendation feed
fails: Evidence 'weakens after creator fixed effects'; clicks not orders
how_to_use: Cold audience: show the result, not the lesson; keep the lesson for people who already follow.
source: Video Design and Product-Link Clicking in Short-Video Commerce, JTAER 2026
doubt: Weakens with creator fixed effects; whole video, not opening.

rule: Cut faster than most people do: Kickstarter videos with quicker shot changes raised more money, and almost nobody cuts too fast.
result: +1 SD shot changes per second = +12.2% funds (p<.01), +1 SD visual jump between shots = +7.0% (p<.01); turning point 3.41 SD above the mean (short videos 4.67, long 2.44); up to +29% predicted at that point
measured_by: Joo, Zo & Kim, Electronic Commerce Research 2026; 5,297 Kickstarter campaigns with video, 13 categories, 2012-2024, fixed effects, observational
holds: Pitch videos on a product page
fails: Not randomised: better-funded teams edit more; not a scrolling feed; the down-turn for visual jump not robust
how_to_use: If a client's product-page film has few cuts, adding cuts is the safe direction; keep long films calmer.
source: Joo, Zo & Kim, How shot-level video structure shapes viewer response, Electronic Commerce Research 2026
doubt: Production quality confound.

rule: The more an ad is passed round, the less it makes each viewer want the product - unless it travels because it is funny or because people talk about the product itself.
result: Exposure alone raises stated purchase intent by 6.6 percentage points; per 1 million more views the ad is on average 10% less persuasive; total persuasion stops growing at 3-4 million views (6% of campaigns got there). Trade-off gone when a top-five comment names the product (coefficient -0.0069 ns, 41% of campaigns) vs -0.0220 (p<.05) when none does; outrageous -0.0225**, not outrageous -0.0152 ns; funny -0.0133 ns, not funny -0.0211**. Very funny beats quite funny (rising curve).
measured_by: Tucker, Marketing Science 34(2) 2015 (author's final manuscript read): 396 consumer-goods video ads of 2010, 24,367 people on Mechanical Turk, half randomly shown the ad, half a placebo ad, forced viewing; stated intent
holds: US consumer goods, big brands; robust to having seen it before, length, category, age, awareness
fails: Intent, not purchase; exposure randomised but views are not, so what makes an ad viral is not randomised; differences funny vs not funny not tested against each other; 2010
how_to_use: If a wild idea does not need the product to work, do not run it for sales. Read the comments of the first 24 hours: if nobody names the product, rebuild the opening round the product.
source: Tucker, The Reach and Persuasiveness of Viral Video Ads, Marketing Science 34(2) 2015, author's manuscript
doubt: 10% of a 6.6-point effect is 0.66 points - real but small per viewer.

rule: Shocking people buys views and loses buyers; making them laugh or showing something beautiful buys both.
result: Joint model: outrageous rating raises views (0.0159, p<.05) and lowers persuasiveness (-0.0355, p<.01); funny raises views (0.0133, p<.10), comments (0.0128, p<.10) and persuasiveness (0.0147, p<.10); visual appeal raises persuasiveness (0.0746, p<.01) but not views
measured_by: Tucker 2015, Table 7, 23,673 respondents, 396 ads, ratings by the respondents
fails: The humour effects are only marginally significant (p<.10)
how_to_use: Beauty of the picture is the surest of the three for wanting the product; use humour second; leave outrage out.
source: Tucker 2015, author's manuscript
doubt: The first round gave humour as the safe exception; visual appeal is the statistically stronger one.

rule: Open with an ordinary creature DOING the impossible, not with a creature that LOOKS impossible: the first is read as wit, the second as an AI mistake.
result: Impossible action vs no opening clip: +1.2 points watched to the end (2.25% vs 1.10%, p<.01), purchases per view +0.001 (p<.05). Impossible look: no gain in watching (+0.002 ns), click rate -0.5 points (p<.05), average view -1.29 s (p<.01). In views that happened, action +1.65 s, look -1.74 s.
measured_by: Zhang, Peng & Tan, Information & Management 64 (2027): field experiment, Douyin + Kuaishou, 10,440 video-days, same product film under five openings; placebo test with 1,000 reshuffles
holds: Useful products (daily goods, condiments, paper); unlabelled clips
fails: Pleasure products (clothes, bags, fresh food): gain -0.9 to -1.0 points; with the AI label the gain falls from 1.2 to 0.2 points; all AI clips get about 43-45% fewer views; conversion numbers tiny and p only <.05; no randomisation of viewers; R2 of conversions 0.011
how_to_use: If the studio makes an AI opening, make the event odd and the creature perfect; weigh the fewer views against more sales per view; platforms that oblige an AI label take most of the watching gain away.
source: Zhang, Peng & Tan, AI error or AI creativity?, Information & Management 64, 2027
doubt: The nearest thing found to a field test of 'event in second 1' with purchases. Most of the sales jump is AI-clip vs none (0.055-0.072% vs 0.002%), not impossible vs plain AI clip. Do not promise money on it; test it.

rule: On a skippable ad, squeezing the joke into the first five seconds makes people like the ad a bit more; on an unskippable ad letting it build makes it funnier. Neither changes liking of the brand.
result: Skippable: ad liking 5.06 vs 4.58 of 7 (p=.045); non-skippable: funniness 4.26 (late) vs 3.63 (early) (p=.02); brand attitude no effect; overall multivariate interaction p=.08
measured_by: Sun, Univ. of Georgia dissertation 2022; study 1 randomised, 264 students (75% women), two real ads re-cut (detergent, home insurance), spike at 4-5 s or 8-10 s; study 2 adults: mediation only for non-skippable
fails: Early-spike gain for skippable ads was NOT significant in study 2; no skipping, clicking or buying result; brand attitude nil
how_to_use: Weak support for moving the laugh before the skip button; do it because it costs nothing, not because it sells.
source: Sun, The effect of arousal spike positions, PhD dissertation, University of Georgia 2022
doubt: The first round presented it as support without the non-replication.

rule: Show the brand in short, repeated flashes instead of one long stay: fewer people leave, with the same total seconds of brand.
result: Re-cut real ads: 67% zapped (many short flashes) vs 74% (few), p=.002, -9.5% relative; 4 of 6 ads moved 9-25%, 2 not at all. Model on 31 ads: -7.9% (2.0-19.1%); a pulsed ad is left even less than an ad with no brand at all (47.2% vs 49.3%, not significant); brand large and steady in the centre raises leaving
measured_by: Teixeira, Wedel & Pieters, Marketing Science 29(5) 2010: eye tracking + zapping of 1,998 people on 31 Dutch TV ads; randomised validation with 130 students, 6 ads
holds: 30 s TV commercials, zapping by key
fails: No sales; moderate changes only (3 to 10 flashes); feed not tested; single brand at the end holds people for 'one or two seconds' at most
how_to_use: Put the name on the object (apron, van, box) and let it pass through the frame several times, under a second each; never park a logo in the centre of the opening.
source: Teixeira, Wedel & Pieters, Moment-to-Moment Optimal Branding in TV Commercials, Marketing Science 2010
doubt: Watching only. It also says a brand that appears late causes more leaving than an early one - the opposite of what is usually quoted from it.

rule: Losing people in the first moments did not hurt Shorts; losing them between 10% and 20% of the way, when the promise should start paying, did.
result: On 'promise' channels 1 SD more leaving at 10-20% went with about 39% fewer views per day (partial r -0.28, -0.17 strictest; N 1,734); losing people at the very start went with MORE views; format channels -0.05
measured_by: SocArXiv preprint 'The Second Decision' 2026; 2,597 Shorts, 11 channels, three creators; exploratory, choices made after seeing the data
fails: Two of eleven channels carry most of it; author owns one; not preregistered; views not sales
how_to_use: After the hook write the first instalment of the answer by second 4-8 of a 40 s video.
source: The Second Decision, SocArXiv 2026 (abstract)
doubt: Abstract only.

rule: Ads whose smile keeps growing to the end and that never make people pull a face of disgust sold more; people's own 'I'd buy it' answers told less.
result: Sorting good sellers from bad: face signals F1 0.745, self-reported liking and purchase intent 0.696, coin-flip 0.610, both together 0.750. Only smile slope and disgust mattered among the facial actions measured; average sellers were left out of the test.
measured_by: McDuff, el Kaliouby, Kodra (Affectiva) with Mars, 2013: 11,000+ face videos of 1,153 people in US, UK, France, Germany, 115 TV ads of 70 brands with single-source short-term sales index; leave-one-ad-out
holds: Mars foods: chocolate, gum and similar
fails: Vendor and advertiser paper, not randomised; differences between categories not tested; a very funny bullying scene scored 'disgust' yet the ad sold
how_to_use: Test an ad on 30 faces: is the smile curve going up at the end, is there any disgust in the opening? Cut a disgust opening even when it stops people.
source: McDuff et al., Do Emotions in Advertising Drive Sales?, Affectiva/Mars 2013
url: local copy affec.pdf (first round); address not re-opened
doubt: Gain over coin flip is 13 points of F1 on good-vs-bad only; significance between models not tested.

rule: When people give you a tenth of a second to two seconds, let the picture say at once what you sell; a riddle is liked least at first and needs ten seconds just to draw level; dressing up as another product starts well and ends worst.
result: After 0.1 s people name the product: plain ad 99%, riddle 27%, false front 1% (89% believe the wrong product). Liking after 0.1 s (5-point): 3.56 / 2.60 / 3.32; after 10 s: 3.30 / 2.92 / 2.76 (plain = riddle, false front below). Replicated in two further experiments (7-point: 0.1 s 5.05/3.86/4.40; 30 s plain 4.84, riddle 4.40, false front least); opinion of the brand follows the same pattern, smaller. Free viewing: riddle 5.53 s, false front 5.73 s, plain 4.45 s.
measured_by: Elsen, PhD thesis Tilburg 2012 (chapter 2 = the JMR 2016 paper's laboratory studies): three randomised experiments, 89 and 78 students plus study 3 (9 ads x 3 types, four exposure times), 100 ms to 30 s
holds: Still ads for food, drink, fragrance, tooth care, hair care, cars, phones
fails: Still pictures, students, liking not buying; a riddle does hold the eye about 1 s longer when people may stay; the published paper's field experiment is not in the thesis pages read
how_to_use: Thumbnail, first frame, outdoor poster, feed ad: product recognisable at a glance. Riddles only where people have already stopped (page, letter). Never bait with another trade's picture.
source: Elsen, Thin and thicker slices, Tilburg dissertation 2012, ch. 2 (basis of Elsen, Pieters & Wedel, Thin Slice Impressions, JMR 2016)
doubt: Text read by OCR; numbers for liking taken from the running text, not the garbled tables. Liking only.

rule: In the first seconds show the product being used; let the brand name come later and shortly - that pairing went with more supermarket sales for TV ads of known packaged goods.
result: Early product introduction linked to improved sales; later brand-name introduction and shorter brand time linked to improved sales; agreed across traditional, AI and machine-learning models. No effect size printed on any open page.
measured_by: Williams (Otago) with Ehrenberg-Bass Institute researchers, Int. J. Market Research 2022: re-analysis of 312 TV ads of 60+ brands of ONE packaged-goods company, five developed markets, single-source household purchases
fails: Unfamiliar brands: the authors say recognition matters more there; observational; one company's data; size of effect unknown to us
how_to_use: Known brand: product working first, name at the close, briefly. Unknown small shop: product first, but do not hide the name.
source: Research Live feature 2023 on Williams et al., Finding creative drivers of advertising effectiveness with modern data analysis, IJMR 2022
doubt: Paper closed; second-hand. 'Product early, brand late' is four findings on one data set that the earlier 2016 analysis of the same ads did not single out.

rule: No single device in a TV ad sells by itself; what was best in 1986 is mostly not best now.
result: 312 TV ads, over 150 creative devices, short-term sales: no single device explains much; many of the most (and least) effective devices differ from the 1986 study
measured_by: Hartnett, Kennedy, Sharp & Greenacre, Journal of Advertising 45(1) 2016; packaged goods, several countries, single-source sales
fails: Abstract only read, no sizes
how_to_use: Never sell a client one magic opening; sell a set of rivals and a test.
source: Hartnett et al., Creative That Sells, J. Advertising 2016 (abstract, Monash page)
doubt: Abstract only; full text closed (UniSA and Monash pages carry no file; her thesis 'Advertisements that sell' is catalogued, not openable).

rule: A hand that really handles the product makes people feel it is half theirs and worth more; a hand beside the product, or a touch that tells nothing, does not.
result: Eight studies with images, GIFs and virtual reality: higher psychological ownership and product valuation; attenuated when the interaction does not represent a diagnostic hand motion; sizes not in the abstract
measured_by: Luangrath, Peck, Hedgcock & Xu, JMR 59(2) 2022, randomised laboratory/online studies; N not given on the open page
fails: Stated value, not sales; not an opening-seconds test
how_to_use: Second 0: fingers press the mattress, run over the worktop, twist the jar - the motion a buyer would use to judge it.
source: Luangrath et al., Observing Product Touch, JMR 2022 (abstract)
doubt: Abstract and AMA interview only.

rule: On a live sales video every strong face - smiling included - went with fewer sales, worst in the middle of the pitch; show less of the face at the start and let it build.
result: 99,451 pitches: each of six emotions has a negative U-shaped effect on sales over time; lowest in the middle; best share of face 'wanes at the start, gradually builds to a crescendo, and eventually ebbs'. Sizes not in abstract.
measured_by: Bharadwaj, Ballings, Naik, Moore & Arat, Journal of Marketing 86(1) 2022; 99,451 livestream pitches matched with actual transactions, observational
holds: One livestream retail platform, one-to-many selling
fails: Not randomised; abstract only; contradicts TikTok Shop finding that enthusiasm helps (1.08x)
how_to_use: Pitch opening on the goods and hands, calm face, energetic voice; keep the big smile for start and end, not the middle.
source: Bharadwaj et al., A New Livestream Retail Analytics Framework, J. Marketing 2022 (abstract)
doubt: Abstract only; no size.

rule: Emotion and memory signals of the first three seconds already tell whether an ad will be liked; understanding and judgement only count late.
result: fMRI, 113 people, 85 video ads, two countries: emotion and memory earliest predictors 'after the first three seconds'; emotion peaks early and falls; social feeling peaks and stays; perception/executive function peak late
measured_by: Chan et al., JMR (abstract), DOI 10.1177/00222437231194319
fails: Liking only; abstract only
how_to_use: Feeling and a person first, argument second.
source: Chan et al., Neural Signals of Video Advertisement Liking, JMR (abstract)
doubt: Full text is on disk (chan2023.txt) but only the abstract was read.

rule: Two clearly different video ads shown to the same audience are worth testing: the better one typically brings the customer for a third less.
result: In advertisers' successful YouTube creative tests of 2019-2020 the better ad had a 30% lower median cost per acquisition; for recall goals 60% higher ad recall. Single case: Decathlon films made per audience +175% incremental online conversions, 64% lower cost per conversion, ROAS +51%
measured_by: Google Ads (Ali Miller), global studies 2019-2020, controlled video experiments; number of tests not given
fails: Only tests with a significant difference are counted, so the 30% is the size WHEN a winner exists; vendor
how_to_use: Sell the client two or three really different openings and a test, not one opinion; text overlay is the cheapest thing to vary.
source: Google Ads & Commerce Blog, Video experiments boost creative performance on YouTube, 6 Apr 2021
doubt: Seller of the tool; winners only.

rule: Short shop videos are watched longer when they show the thing in use and state facts; being pleasant or pretty helps about a third as much.
result: Average watch time: showing use +0.568 s, describing features +0.380 s, beauty +0.195 s, pleasant feeling +0.171 s (all p<.01; videos 16.6 s long on average, R2 .166). By goods: showing use strongest for dear look-alike goods (+1.072), facts strongest for variety goods (+0.770) and nil for habitual goods; pleasantness only for habitual (+0.311) and variety (+0.149)
measured_by: Guo et al., ACM TMIS 15(4) 2024; 23,001 Taobao shop videos, 10,083 creators, five annotators each, mixed-effects regression
fails: Watching not buying; not randomised; under 5% of the film's length; whole video, not opening
how_to_use: Shop clip: first shot = the thing doing its job; add one fact; do not spend on mood first.
source: Guo et al., Analyzing and Predicting Consumer Response to Short Videos in E-Commerce, ACM TMIS 2024
doubt: The effect is half a second.

rule: Ordinary customers talking to the camera on a brief got fewer clicks but more buyers than the brand's polished ads for the same book.
result: Conversion rate higher (Z=23.2, p about 2e-119), return on ad spend higher (p<.01), click-through rate LOWER (Z=-18.0, p<.01). Rates only in tables not in the open text. Working method: each creator films one video with three different first-three-second openings, a small A/B test picks one.
measured_by: Ntousi, Lazaris, Katiaj & Koukopoulos, Systems 13(2) 124, 2025; 26 creator vs 41 brand Meta campaigns for one book, Greece
fails: Not randomised: campaigns ran at different times to different people; brand ads were photos or videos, creator ads already the winner of an A/B test, so the comparison is unfair
how_to_use: Copy the method (one body, three openings, small test), not the claim.
source: Ntousi et al., Directed Consumer-Generated Content, Systems 2025
doubt: The first round called it a field experiment without saying that the creator ads were pre-selected winners and the campaigns were not randomised.

rule: Acting-now messages bring visits and sales; facts or feelings bring fewer clicks yet more sales for most brands - so clicks alone pick the wrong ad.
result: Action-focus raises site traffic and sales; information- and emotion-focus lower traffic while raising purchases; net positive for most brands
measured_by: Liaukonyte, Teixeira & Wilbur, Marketing Science 2015 (author's version Nov 2014): $3.4bn of TV ads, 20 brands, purchases in two-minute and two-hour windows, quasi-experiment
fails: Whole ads, not openings; only the abstract of this copy was read by me
how_to_use: Judge a factual opening by orders within two hours and after, never by click rate.
source: Liaukonyte, Teixeira & Wilbur, Television Advertising and Online Shopping, 2015 (abstract)
doubt: Abstract; figures $3.4bn/20 brands from the first round's reading, not re-checked.

rule: Change of picture has a best middle: too little bores, too much confuses.
result: Inverted U between visual variety and effectiveness in three studies, over 3,000 TV and social ads, plus a laboratory experiment; no numbers in the abstract
measured_by: Kinzinger, Tetzlaff, Krugmann & Hartmann, EMAC 2025
fails: Abstract only
how_to_use: Vary shots, keep one subject.
source: Kinzinger et al., Valuable visual variety, EMAC 2025 (abstract)
doubt: No sizes.

rule: The right reason to buy matters more than pretty design: two good-looking ads for the same thing can sell almost twenty times apart.
result: 19-1/2 times as much merchandise as another ad for the same product; same space, same publication, both photographic
measured_by: John Caples, one mail-order test; N of orders not given
holds: mail order, same product, same space, same publication
fails: one extreme case, wording not printed
how_to_use: Spend most of the time choosing which wish to speak to; test appeals before polishing words.
doubt: single case, both wordings not shown
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 4

rule: The opening line carries half to three quarters of an ad's answers.
result: the headline is 50 to 75 percent of the advertisement
measured_by: Don Belding, trade-magazine article, from inquiry returns; N not given
fails: no table given
how_to_use: Give the first line most of the writing time.
doubt: figure without data
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 13

rule: Ads that bring the most questions usually bring the most sales too, if the free gift is the same in all of them.
result: five million inquiries received by 165 firms over a period of 12 years
measured_by: Daniel Starch, N=5,000,000 inquiries, 165 firms, 12 years
holds: controlled tests with identical subordinated offers
fails: when the headline gives away a free gift (many inquiries, few worthwhile leads)
how_to_use: You may judge openings by qualified inquiries, as long as the freebie is the same in every variant.
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 11

rule: Promise something the reader wants first, give news second, use pure curiosity last.
result: For every curiosity headline that succeeds in getting results, a dozen will fail; of ten very successful headlines all ten offered something wanted, four added curiosity, four a quick easy way, two news
measured_by: John Caples, keyed mail-order headlines; N = ten headlines for the count
fails: a few curiosity headlines win too (What's wrong in this picture?)
how_to_use: Put the benefit in every opening, and add curiosity or news on top of it rather than instead of it.
doubt: 'a dozen' is a manner of speaking, not a count
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 17, 26

rule: Experienced advertising people guess the winning ad wrong about half the time, so test instead of voting.
result: About 50 percent of the judgments of members of 14 advertising clubs were wrong against the actual sales results
measured_by: 14 advertising clubs judging mail order ads of known results; number of judges not given
fails: judges and ads not listed
how_to_use: Never let a meeting pick the opening; run two.
doubt: original study not named
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 28

rule: Openings that only tease, with no news and no benefit, are the ones that die.
result: ten tested headlines were outstanding failures: all ten primarily curiosity, none gave news, none offered a benefit, seven were negative
measured_by: John Caples, keyed ads run in a publication used for earlier tests; N=10 headlines
fails: counts ten chosen failures, not a sample
how_to_use: Check every opening: is there a benefit or news in it? If it only teases or only frightens, rewrite.
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 29-30

rule: A promise that sounds too good brings few answers.
result: 'To men and women who want to work less and earn more' did not bring many replies
measured_by: a correspondence school's keyed test; N not given
fails: the reason is the author's reading
how_to_use: Put a believable, specific size on the promise.
doubt: single failed ad
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 31

rule: Once one promise wins, put it in the opening of every ad; hidden in the text it does little.
result: eleven full-page ads in one year: the five with the winning appeal in the headline brought 502, 511, 550, 666 and 867 replies; the six without it brought 191 to 263; the appeal 'continued to work for several years thereafter'
measured_by: John Caples, one client's 11 magazine full pages, coupon counts; N=4,412 replies in all [sum mine]
holds: one client, magazine pages, coupon replies
fails: client and appeal are not named; publications/issues differed
how_to_use: Find the winning promise, then write many openings around that one promise. Best of the losers (263) had it only in a sub-heading.
doubt: not a split run; the appeal itself is not told
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 74-76

rule: Name the actual item, year and price instead of general praise.
result: three times as many customers answered the ads
measured_by: used-car dealer, actual count; N not given
fails: one dealer
how_to_use: Open with the concrete item and its price.
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 82

rule: The ad that professionals praise most may sell nothing.
result: 'Letters wives don't write to their unsuccessful husbands' got more praise than any business-school ad in years and was an unqualified failure
measured_by: coupon returns, business school; N not given
fails: single case
how_to_use: Do not scold the buyer in the opening; applause from colleagues is no evidence.
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 79-80

rule: The same kind of ad can stop four times as many passers-by as another; count it before you print.
result: of two savings posters one stopped 9 in 1,000 and the other 34; of two trust posters 6 and 16; some stopped one person in ten
measured_by: large bank: observers counting passers and stoppers; four branches almost identical
holds: posters in bank lobbies and windows
fails: stopping is not buying; posters' wording not given
how_to_use: Hang two versions in the shop window for a day each and count who stops.
doubt: bank unnamed
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 92

rule: Take what worked and repeat it: a good ad stays good for years.
result: Bruce Barton's 'A wonderful two years' trip at full pay' ran seven years
measured_by: coupon returns, Alexander Hamilton Institute; N not given
fails: some ads wear out; watch the cost per reply
how_to_use: Do not retire a winning opening because you are bored; retire it when the numbers fall.
doubt: single case
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 118

rule: The ads that give the most facts about the thing sell the most.
result: a large number of successful retail ads compared with unsuccessful ones: the ads that tell the largest number of facts make the most sales
measured_by: unnamed study of retail ads; N 'large number'
fails: figures not given
how_to_use: After the opening, pile true facts; open with the most surprising one.
doubt: no counts
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 119

rule: More than half of the articles in the world's largest-selling magazine open with a story.
result: Over half of the Reader's Digest articles begin with a story (35 articles in the first issue counted, then several more issues)
measured_by: John Caples, content count; 35 articles + more issues
holds: magazine articles whose editors test titles
fails: it counts what editors choose, not what readers finished
how_to_use: Open with a time, a place and a person doing something; few adjectives; arouse a question.
doubt: a count of practice, not a test
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 104-106

rule: One exact number is believed; the same number rounded is taken as boasting.
result: '52.7%' brought 150 carload orders in weeks; changed to 'over 50%' demand fell to a fraction
measured_by: building-material maker, before/after; 150 carload orders
fails: not a simultaneous split
how_to_use: Open with the number exactly as measured, decimals included.
doubt: company not named
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 142-143

rule: Do not announce in the first contact that a salesman will call.
result: To do so will cut down your coupon returns at least 75 percent
measured_by: John Caples from coupon experience; N not given
fails: no test printed; hiding a call you do plan can break trust
how_to_use: Offer the booklet without any call and do not call unless asked.
doubt: figure without data; CAUTION: the book advises hiding the call — do not deceive
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 157

rule: Only five of more than 700 large ads used plain facts, so facts stand out.
result: five of more than 700 large-space ads in the December 1995 issues of 14 of America's most popular consumer magazines
measured_by: editor F. Hahn, content count; N=700+ ads, 14 magazines
fails: counts use, not sales
how_to_use: Facts are still a free place to stand out.
doubt: no result attached
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 141

rule: In a letter parcel, several separate pieces beat one booklet with everything in it.
result: all large users of direct mail such as insurance companies, correspondence schools, record clubs and book publishers have found the other method (separate pieces) more effective
measured_by: large mailers' practice as reported by Caples; N not given
fails: no figures
how_to_use: Give each piece its own opening that sells at a glance: seven chances instead of one.
doubt: no figures
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 153

rule: Say the free thing in the headline when you want more answers.
result: 'Free booklet tells how to retire on an income' increases response over 'How to retire on an income'
measured_by: John Caples from inquiry ads; N not given
fails: more answers of lower quality possible; figures not given here
how_to_use: Put the offer itself in the first line when leads are the aim.
doubt: no figure
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 169

rule: People who telephone buy more than people who write.
result: sold one out of five people who wrote for a catalog, but one out of two who telephoned
measured_by: adult education school; N not given
fails: one school
how_to_use: Make the opening lead to a call or chat, not only to a form.
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 176

rule: The same ad can double its replies by the month, and gain 40% by the day.
result: January pulled twice as many replies as August; Sunday newspaper ads pulled 40 percent more replies than daily
measured_by: one test each, couponed ads; N not given
fails: Sunday circulation also larger
how_to_use: Judge an opening only against another that ran in the same week.
doubt: single tests
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 181

rule: In a series with the same offer, one ad will often pull twice the others through a better headline or picture.
result: will pull twice as many inquiries as the other ads
measured_by: John Caples; N not given
fails: no list
how_to_use: Run several openings on one offer before spending.
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 179

rule: Adding the buyer's name or one benefit word to a good line lifts it by a fifth to a quarter.
result: 'Car owners!' +20%; 'Dry Up' +27% (380 vs 297); 'Fix' for 'Repair' +20% orders
measured_by: newspaper split runs and one mail-order case; N given only for hay fever (677)
holds: small print ads, samples and orders
fails: Caples says only 'in a number of cases' — other changes did nothing
how_to_use: Take the opening that already works and test one small change: who it is for, what it does, an easier verb.
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 194-195

rule: The magazine's sales people shorten and sharpen titles for the cover.
result: seventeen before/after pairs, e.g. 'Hot Tips on Heating Your Home' became 'How to Cut Fuel Bills'; 'Backyard Gardens Are Back in Style' became 'How to Start a Backyard Garden'
measured_by: circulation departments' practice; no sales figures
fails: no copy sales are given
how_to_use: Rewrite every title once more as if it had to sell the thing on a counter.
doubt: practice, not test
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 196-197

rule: Brides, babies, animals, famous people, odd costumes, odd situations, story pictures, catastrophes and news pictures are noticed most.
result: Hundreds of readership surveys
measured_by: readership surveys, 'hundreds'; N not given
fails: High attention does not mean sales: unrelated bride or baby in a car ad stops the wrong people
how_to_use: Use one only if it belongs to the thing you sell.
doubt: no figures
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 203-204

rule: Men look at ads with men in them, women at ads with women.
result: observation from readership surveys
measured_by: readership surveys; N not given
fails: no figures
how_to_use: Show the buyer his own kind; do not use a woman's figure to stop men (it stops the wrong mood).
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 204

rule: The pictures that sell: the product, the product in use, the reward, the ambition reached, an enlarged detail, a dramatic picture that belongs to it.
result: based on sales tests of advertisements
measured_by: sales tests as reported by Caples; N not given
fails: no figures
how_to_use: Choose the first frame from these six.
doubt: no figures
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 204-205

rule: A face looking straight at the reader often outsells other pictures and fits the smallest space.
result: this type of illustration often brings more sales than other types
measured_by: mail-order advertisers' experience; N not given
fails: no figures
how_to_use: In small formats use the customer's own face, eyes to camera.
doubt: no figures
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 209

rule: In ten tested pairs the winner always spoke of the reader's own gain in plain words; the loser was clever, vague, or praised the product.
result: 10 of 10 pairs; differences by a wide margin; losers used only once
measured_by: John Caples, ten keyed pairs; N of replies not given
holds: mail order print, courses, insurance, publications
fails: pairs chosen to teach; no ratios
how_to_use: Before testing, check each opening: is it about the reader, plain, specific?
doubt: selected pairs
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 224-233

rule: Easy-to-explain things sell in small ads; hard-to-believe things need a long one.
result: reducing belt paid in 60-line ads and not in full pages; hair treatment paid in full pages and not in 60 lines; music course paid in every size down to one inch
measured_by: John Caples's agency, keyed ads; N not given
fails: three products
how_to_use: If a picture explains it, go short; if people doubt it, the opening must lead into long proof.
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 216-217

rule: People's opinions and their purchases disagree: opinion tests favour clever ads and ads with pictures; sales tests often favour simple and all-type ones.
result: where both tests were applied to the same ads, they did not always obtain the same results
measured_by: Caples's experience; N not given
fails: no counts; also people hide embarrassing reasons (bad breath)
how_to_use: Do not ask customers which opening they like; count what they do. If asking, show two, never one or three.
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 238-239

rule: Speak of the comfort the person wants, not of the engineer's best feature.
result: 'cool, quiet bedroom—even on hot nights' averaged two and a half times the calls of 'Get rid of that humidity'
measured_by: alternating ads over weeks, 500,000-circulation paper; N not given
holds: home appliance, local newspaper, phone calls
fails: one product
how_to_use: Translate the maker's proudest feature into how the buyer's evening changes.
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 249-250

rule: Change one small thing at a time: picture above the headline +8%, a smile +25%, two words +20%, a 'free booklet' line above the coupon +5%.
result: 8%, 25%, 20% and 5% more replies
measured_by: four newspaper split-runs; N not given
holds: newspapers, identical ads but for one change
fails: N not given; the 5% and 8% may be chance
how_to_use: First place the headline under the picture, let the person smile, name the buyer, repeat the offer near the button.
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 263

rule: Writing many headlines for one same text can show one that pulls four times the usual.
result: 36 headlines in two weeks on the same copy: one exceeded the control by 300 percent and another by 200 percent; became the basis of a successful national campaign
measured_by: four split-run newspapers, same control ad, patent medicine, hidden $1 sample; N not given
fails: winning words are not printed
how_to_use: Write dozens of openings to the same body, run each against one fixed control, and keep the two giants.
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 266-267

rule: About a hundred answers for each version is enough to judge; ten is not.
result: a hundred replies is about right; ten may not be dependable; a thousand is needlessly costly
measured_by: agency experience
fails: today's statistics ask for more when differences are small
how_to_use: Do not name a winner before about 100 replies per version.
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 244

rule: Two reasons to buy the same cosmetic, on cards in half the buses each, differed by 65 percent, and the newspaper test agreed.
result: 65 percent more replies from one card than from the other
measured_by: two half-showings on one bus line, two months; N not given
fails: the book does not say which appeal won (social popularity or a named skin ailment)
how_to_use: A winner in one cheap place usually wins in the other; test where it is cheap.
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 255

rule: One of several postcards with a new reason to buy can pull half as much again as the rest.
result: nearly 50 percent more replies than any of the other cards
measured_by: six headlines on double postcards by mail; N not given
holds: mailed postcards with hidden sample offer
fails: product was cigars, wording not given
how_to_use: Test six reasons on postcards or story cards before the campaign.
doubt: tobacco product
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 253

rule: The straight offer beats the thoughtful question when the person has an urgent need.
result: the plain 'how you can get' headline brought two and a half times as many calls as the 'when can it help you?' headline
measured_by: two newspaper ads, calls counted by the name asked for; N not given
fails: one test; the product was an interest loan, so only the shape may be used
how_to_use: For a burst pipe or toothache say at once how to get it fixed; no philosophy.
doubt: product is a finance-company loan: no opening row is made of it
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 251

rule: A place in the paper, the season and the ad itself each can double or halve results.
result: some ads of a dozen produce two or three times as much business as others; special positions often add 50 to 100 percent
measured_by: John Caples; N not given
fails: no table
how_to_use: Compare openings only in the same place and week.
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 268

rule: A headline that names its offer as information, plus a chapter of real advice in the catalog, pulls better.
result: a garden-seed advertiser made his seed catalogue ads pull better by putting in a chapter of gardening advice
measured_by: seed advertiser; N not given
fails: no figure
how_to_use: Put real help into the free thing and say so in the opening.
doubt: no figure
source: John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods, 5th ed., rev. Fred E. Hahn, Prentice Hall 1997, p. 173

rule: When the shopper’s first question is "which one is for me?", the first screen should let him choose.
result: Thomas Pink shirt finder +12.18% purchases (136,000 visitors, 30 days); flavour links +29% orders (139 against 107, 98%); category tiles iTokri +12.82% conversion; Xtrema "shop by category" +40.41% category views (N 7,937); EcoFoil help box +86% purchases
measured_by: Practicology, GrowthRock, ConvertPolo, Enavi, Clickstop; five separate A/B tests
holds: shops with many kinds, buyers who cannot judge terms, phones
fails: "Shop by Vehicle" alone lost at Aeromotive; "Shop by Category" moved under the hero lost 6.2% (Clean Commit); GrowthRock’s quiz left conversion flat and was later removed
how_to_use: for a catalogue client, test one chooser as the first words ("Find my …", "Which … are you?") beside the product claim
source: Wingify/VWO success story, Thomas Pink; with GrowthRock, Convert, VWO pages in the same folder
doubt: the finder came together with the removal of a content block; most of the others give no N

rule: Write search-ad headlines as a sentence: capital on the first word only.
result: in 9 of 12 ad sets the sentence-case ads had the higher click rate, by 6% to 64%
measured_by: ORYX Rent a Car, 12 pairs of Google ads in four groups, three months; N not given
fails: 3 of the 12 sets went the other way or were level
how_to_use: write the search headline in sentence case and test it against Title Case
source: MarketingSherpa, Discovering What Works in Marketing, 10 Nov 2020
doubt: one advertiser; clicks only

rule: A clever tail can kill a winning line: end on the result.
result: "Say Yes when a client asks you to review FIVE MILLION separate documents." 9 leads of 948 clicks; the same line plus "And smile." 0 of 888
measured_by: MarketingExperiments, A/B/C split run on AdWords traffic
fails: not repeated elsewhere
how_to_use: cut the last two words of every hook and test the cut line
source: MarketingExperiments, Site Headlines Tested, 2006
doubt: nine leads in all

beat: an ordinary film of the same account, posted within 35 days
doubt: views on TikTok, not sales; the difference is small; labels by one model over both sets, by a second over the first
holds: short films on a small maker's or shop's own account; unpaid; seen by strangers
measured_by: 341 pairs from 341 accounts (131 and 210, two separate draws), every film labelled blind and alone by GPT-6.2 Sol from five frames of the first 3.5 seconds and the first words
