rule: On your own account open on something that is already happening, not on a face that talks to the lens.
result: an action already under way or half done in the first second: 61 of 100 films that went round, 51 of 100 ordinary films of the same accounts (83 pairs against 50; both draws alike, 31:17 and 52:33; a second model 30:13 on the first); a face that talks to the camera in the first second: 23 against 30 of 100 (26 pairs against 49; 9:18 and 17:31)
how_to_use: begin the film one second later: the hand already cutting, the pour already running, the door already opening; the face comes after

beat: an ordinary film of the same account, posted within 35 days
doubt: views on TikTok, not sales; the difference is small; labels by one model over both sets, by a second over the first
holds: short films on a small maker's or shop's own account; unpaid; seen by strangers
measured_by: 341 pairs from 341 accounts (131 and 210, two separate draws), every film labelled blind and alone by GPT-6.2 Sol from five frames of the first 3.5 seconds and the first words
source: the hook library's own measurement, 25 November 2026
rule: Let the thing itself, best an uncommon one, fill the first frame.
result: the thing itself fills most of the first frame: 46 against 40 of 100 (44 pairs against 25); one uncommon object or result whose making, inside or price one wants to know: 23 against 17 of 100 (53 pairs against 31); stronger in the second draw than in the first
how_to_use: the product, the work or the animal large in the first frame, not the room and not the maker

beat: an ordinary film of the same account, posted within 35 days
doubt: views on TikTok, not sales; the difference is small; labels by one model over both sets, by a second over the first
holds: short films on a small maker's or shop's own account; unpaid; seen by strangers
measured_by: 341 pairs from 341 accounts (131 and 210, two separate draws), every film labelled blind and alone by GPT-6.2 Sol from five frames of the first 3.5 seconds and the first words
source: the hook library's own measurement, 25 November 2026
rule: Spend the effort on the first picture's action, not on the form of the first sentence: pace, words and wording patterns did not tell the winner from the same account's ordinary film.
result: alike in films that went round and in ordinary ones of the same account: a question left open 84 and 82 of 100, a number or price 30 and 30, a story begun 31 and 29, words on the screen 80 and 80, two things set against each other 21 and 20, naming a kind of person 17 and 16; by code over the same 341 pairs no difference in movement, cuts, loudness, light, contrast, number of words, length of the film
how_to_use: a plain first line is enough; change the first picture before you change the words

rule: Showing the photo of the real customer beside his words doubles sign-ups; the person's sex or home town does not matter.
result: 2.9% -> 6.4%; sex and distance made no significant difference
measured_by: BIT trial at HMRC, about 1,500 employees
holds: message from colleagues inside one organisation
fails: not tested with strangers
how_to_use: Never print a testimonial without the face; do not waste effort matching the face's gender to the reader.
source: Behavioural Insights Team / Cabinet Office, Applying behavioural insights to charitable giving, 2013

rule: Put the help you already did for the person, with your name and good luck, in the invitation text.
result: turn-up 26.8% (reciprocity) vs 17.4% (names) vs 14.8% (name of person only) vs 10.5% (plain details)
measured_by: BIT randomised trial, Bedford Jobcentre, n = 1,224
fails: small sample per arm
how_to_use: 'I have booked you a place at 10.30 ... Good luck, Sarah' beats a plain event notice; say only what was really done.
source: Behavioural Insights Team, Update Report 2013-2015, 2015

rule: Taking the moving picture carousel off the top of the page raised sign-ups.
result: carousel cost 0.5 percentage points of sign-ups in every version; removing it added 3,000 registrations; best page = health benefit + one testimonial, no carousel
measured_by: BIT/PHE randomised multi-page trial (Stoptober), n = 345,469
holds: sign-up page with a single action
fails: not tested on shop pages
how_to_use: First screen of a landing page: one benefit line, one real testimonial, one button; no rotating banner.
source: Behavioural Insights Team, Update Report 2013-2015, 2015

rule: A small unexpected gift before the ask works again a year later, but about half as well on people who got it last year.
result: effect fell by roughly a half on repeat receivers
measured_by: BIT trial, n = 6,833
fails: weakens with repetition
how_to_use: Change the surprise every time; keep the same surprise for new customers.
source: Behavioural Insights Team, Update Report 2013-2015, 2015

rule: A talk about the good life it brings won; the same facts in a leaflet to the young person put them off.
result: interest 47.4% after a talk; written information to pupils made them significantly less likely to want to apply
measured_by: BIT Somerset trial, n = 1,440
fails: stated intention, not enrolment
how_to_use: Open with a person telling the life it gave him, not with a fact sheet.
source: Behavioural Insights Team, Update Report 2013-2015, 2015

rule: A stock photo of a group of people can undo a winning sentence: the same 'thousands of people' line won alone and lost under the photo.
result: line alone 2.9%, line + NHS logo 2.9%, line + people photo 2.2%, control 2.3%
measured_by: BIT/GDS randomised trial, 1,085,322 visitors
fails: a real named colleague's photo did the opposite (HMRC trial 2.9% -> 6.4%)
how_to_use: Use the real person's photo or none; never a bought group picture.
source: Cabinet Office BIT / NHSBT / GDS / DVLA, Applying Behavioural Insights to Organ Donation: preliminary results, 2013

rule: Saying how FEW people give can raise giving to a shared thing people want to keep (Wikipedia); for most other things say how many.
result: Wikipedia donations rise when it says how few donate (no figure printed)
measured_by: Wikipedia's own tests as reported by BIT
fails: elsewhere, saying many misbehave makes more misbehave
how_to_use: Only for a shared good ('Only 1 in 50 listeners pays for this station'); never to shame a customer.
source: Behavioural Insights Team, EAST: Four Simple Ways to Apply Behavioural Insights (revised edition, 2024)

rule: Make the request simple: key message in the first sentence or subject line, one action, one contact, the rest out.
result: making a request easier to understand often gives about a 5% increase in response; New York court summons redesign cut no-shows 13%; Belgian tax letters up to 23% more paid
measured_by: BIT, dozens of trials
fails: same readability but no link to the reader's own life is understood 19% less
how_to_use: First sentence = what to do and what it means for you; plain words are not enough, tie it to his own money or day.
source: Behavioural Insights Team, EAST: Four Simple Ways to Apply Behavioural Insights (revised edition, 2024)

rule: 'You are already entered; claim it only if you have signed up' draws more than 'sign up to enter'.
result: regret draw 31% more effective than a normal draw and over twice no draw; 1.8% -> 2.3% (not significant at usual levels)
measured_by: BIT, Gresham Oregon; N not read
holds: free draw on a utility bill
fails: not statistically secure
how_to_use: Not for us as a prize draw (chance-based); take only the frame 'it is already yours, collect it by...' with a certain gift.
source: Behavioural Insights Team, Update Report 2016-17, 2017
doubt: A lottery: outside our boundaries; only the 'already yours' frame is noted

rule: A short prompt letter moves even expensive choices: early mortgage repayment letters with the saving in money.
result: letter readers more than four times as likely to make a repayment; high vs low suggested amount made no significant difference
measured_by: BIT Singapore, nearly 5,000 households
fails: size of suggested amount did not matter
how_to_use: 'Do X now and save Y' works as an opening for big decisions too; take the frame, not the loan product.
source: Behavioural Insights Team, Update Report 2016-17, 2017

rule: One personal thing in a short text is enough: the name beat the amount, and name plus amount was no better than the name.
result: average order in both phases: name > name+amount > amount > standard > none
measured_by: 5,450 people, two phases
fails: differences between the personalised versions are not statistically secure
how_to_use: Put the first name first, then one fact; do not stack two personal details.
source: Haynes, Green, Gallagher, John, Torgerson, Collection of Delinquent Fines: An Adaptive Randomized Trial, 2013 (J. Policy Analysis and Management)

rule: To a business, a tip that prevents the mistake they just made pays better than 'most firms pay on time'.
result: both won; educational letter +15% payments and beat the norm letter (+6 points)
measured_by: BIT/HMRC randomised trial, corporation tax debtors
how_to_use: Open a letter to a firm with the one mistake that costs them, and how to avoid it.
source: Behavioural Insights Team, Update Report 2015-16, 2016

rule: From an institution, plain expected wording beats clever, surprising or chatty wording.
result: messages congruent with what people expect did better (beta 0.48, P < 0.03); 'reserved for you' reminders did better (beta 0.41, P = 0.05); a picture joke was among the least effective
measured_by: 47,306 patients, 19 messages; repeated with 689,693 at Walmart
holds: messages from a doctor or pharmacy the person already uses
fails: not a cold advertisement; Denver's joke e-mail line won for a city
how_to_use: Reminders to existing customers: plain, as from the business itself, 'yours is reserved'. Keep the joke for strangers' feeds.
source: Milkman et al., A megastudy of text-based nudges ... upcoming doctor's appointment, PNAS 2021

rule: Experts cannot pick the winning line; test it. And send it twice on different days.
result: neither experts nor lay people named the winner; two-day reminders did best; all 22 beat nothing (+2.0 points on average, 6.8%)
measured_by: 689,693 people
fails: two texts two hours apart were among the weakest (+1.2 to +1.4)
how_to_use: Always two sends, about three days apart; pick the winner by numbers.
source: Milkman et al., A 680,000-person megastudy of nudges to encourage vaccination in pharmacies, PNAS 2022

rule: '75% of guests do it' is not stronger than a plain polite request everywhere: in Germany both beat no card, equally.
result: Study 1 N = 724, Study 2 N = 204: norm card no better than standard card; both raised reuse over no message
measured_by: Two hotels, randomised
fails: the US result (44% vs 35%) was not repeated
how_to_use: Use the true local number when most people do not yet expect it; where nearly everyone does it, spend the line on something else.
source: Bohner & Schlueter, A Room with a Viewpoint Revisited, PLoS ONE 9(8), 2014

rule: Never open with how many people do the wrong thing: it makes more people do it.
result: theft 7.92% under 'Many past visitors have removed ...' vs 4.00% under the other three signs together
measured_by: 2,655 visitors, 1,140 pieces
holds: signs where the bad act happens
fails: single park; no no-sign control in this paper
how_to_use: 'Most people forget their check-up' is banned as a first line; say what most do right or say the plain don't.
source: Cialdini et al., Managing social norms for persuasive impact, Social Influence 1(1), 2006

rule: The sticky note wins because of the handwritten personal request on it, not its colour; for a long task a name and initials on it help more.
result: blank note 43% (no different from 34% none); written note 69%; long survey: none 13%, note 40%, personalised note 67%
measured_by: Studies 2 and 4, 105 and 180 people
fails: short task: personal note no better than plain note
how_to_use: Big ask: write the name and sign it. Small ask: a short handwritten thank-you line is enough.
source: Garner, Post-It Note Persuasion: A Sticky Influence, J. Consumer Psychology 15(3), 2005

rule: The exact number wins over the same thought in general words.
result: 'costs NHS £160 approx' 8.2% missed vs 'wastes NHS money' 9.9%
measured_by: 9,848 appointments, second trial
fails: '9 out of 10 people attend' did not differ from control here
how_to_use: Replace 'saves you money' by the one true sum the reader did not know.
source: Hallsworth et al., Stating Appointment Costs in SMS Reminders Reduces Missed Hospital Appointments, PLoS ONE 2015

rule: The exact percentage beats the round fraction for the same fact: '88% of people agree' moved twice as many as 'nine out of ten agree'.
result: +3.4 points vs +1.7 points (p = 0.02)
measured_by: HMRC second experiment, 2012
holds: statement of what people think is right
fails: what people DO still beat what people approve by 1.44 points
how_to_use: Print the true exact figure (88%), not the rounded one.
source: Hallsworth, List, Metcalfe, Vlaev, The Behavioralist as Tax Collector, J. Public Economics 2017 (WRAP copy)

rule: In the biggest letter test, loss wording did not beat gain wording.
result: gain and loss public-service lines both +1.6 points
measured_by: about 17,000 per letter
fails: organ donors: loss beat gain (3.1 vs 2.9)
how_to_use: Do not assume 'you lose' is stronger than 'you get'; test both.
source: Hallsworth, List, Metcalfe, Vlaev, The Behavioralist as Tax Collector, J. Public Economics 2017 (WRAP copy)

rule: 'Pennies a day' is not always right: for a gift of a full year's support, '750 rupees a month' beat '25 rupees a day'.
result: monthly ask +71% donors, +66% money
measured_by: 184,396 letters, HelpAge India
holds: one yearly sum shown as monthly vs daily, charity
fails: saving app: daily 29.9% vs monthly 7.1%
how_to_use: Daily when the buyer really pays little by little; monthly when the amount is a considered commitment. Test.
source: Sudhir, Roy, Cherian, Do Sympathy Biases Induce Charitable Giving?, Cowles 1940 (Marketing Science 2016)

rule: Saying that a match exists brings more givers; making the match bigger (2:1, 3:1) brings nothing more.
result: +19% money per letter, +22% givers with any match; ratios 1:1, 2:1, 3:1 no different
measured_by: 50,083 past givers, randomised mailing
fails: lab and other charities differ
how_to_use: One clear doubling line is enough; do not raise the bonus before testing the plain one.
source: Karlan & List, Does Price Matter in Charitable Giving?, NBER 12338, 2006 (AER 2007)

rule: 'Most ordered' must be a real count of what people bought; just putting names forward does nothing. It works most on people new to the place.
result: +13-18% vs no significant effect; stronger for infrequent customers (paper)
measured_by: 13 restaurants, Beijing
how_to_use: Print the count and the period ('last week, 412 plates') on the card, for first-timers.
source: Cai, Chen, Fang, Observational Learning, NBER 13516 (AER 2009)

rule: A 5-cent charge changed behaviour where a 5-cent reward did nothing.
result: tax: bag use 82% -> about 40% (-42 points); bonus: 82% vs 84%
measured_by: Washington DC area supermarkets, observed shoppers
fails: 98% noticed the tax, only 52% the bonus
how_to_use: Write the small sum as what it costs to do without, not as a bonus ('Cup 20p' beats '20p off with your cup').
source: Homonoff, Can Small Incentives Have Large Effects?, AEJ Policy 2018 (working copy)

rule: Announcing a visit with a 'do not disturb' box lets unwilling people out; small gifts given from pressure vanish, money quality stays.
result: flyer: door opened 10% less, with opt-out box 25% less; giving -30%, all among gifts under $10
measured_by: door-to-door field experiment, Chicago, thousands of households
how_to_use: For real customers give the way out early; those who stay mean it.
source: DellaVigna, List, Malmendier, Testing for Altruism and Social Pressure, NBER 15629 (QJE 2012)

rule: Cut the praise and the reasons: two thirds fewer words brought 80% more answers, though most people bet on the long one.
result: 4.8% vs 2.7%; 165 of 166 professionals would handle the short one first; 67% of 148 people predicted the long one would win
measured_by: 7,002 people
holds: a request by e-mail to busy people
fails: long sales letters to people already interested are another matter
how_to_use: First e-mail to a stranger under 50 words; name, want, link.
source: Rogers & Lasky-Fink, When Writing for Busy Readers, Less Is More, Behavioral Scientist, 2023

rule: Write to parents and customers at fifth-grade level, short and on their side.
result: rewritten school letters about 40% more effective at cutting absences (later paper); 382-word, tenth-grade, threatening letter lost
measured_by: Randomised, 130,000 students
fails: several things changed at once (length, tone, level)
how_to_use: Read the opening aloud to a twelve-year-old before it is sent.
source: Rogers & Lasky-Fink, Write shorter messages, The Boston Globe, 2020

rule: Even randomly deleting every other sentence of a money-asking e-mail raised gifts.
result: about 20% more donations (as told in the podcast; the book's figure was not seen)
measured_by: US party committee test, about 700,000 recipients
holds: e-mail fund-raising to an existing list
fails: second-hand; check the book
how_to_use: Before sending, strike half; if the ask still stands, send the half.
source: The Consumer Behavior Lab, podcast transcript on Writing for Busy Readers (Shotton & Flicker)

rule: Never put the dish in a box called 'vegetarian' and never lead with meat-free, vegan, low-fat or healthy.
result: meat eaters 56% less likely to order from a 'vegetarian' box (LSE); 'vegan' the least appealing of 21 labels (35% less likely to buy, survey)
measured_by: LSE 2016 online menu study, as told by WRI; survey by Morning Consult
fails: France: healthier rated tastier; the LSE paper's box effect is in infrequent vegetarians only for the reverse direction
how_to_use: Name what the buyer gets and where it comes from.
source: World Resources Institute (Better Buying Lab), It's All in a Name: How to Boost the Sales of Plant-Based Menu Items, 2019

rule: Taste names beat merely cheerful names and work better where the food is really good.
result: taste-focused > labels with only positive words, > fancy words, > lists of ingredients; greater at schools with tastier recipes
measured_by: 5 universities, 137,842 decisions
holds: one dish among several at a counter
fails: weak recipes
how_to_use: Name cooking method + place + flavour; about six words; never over-promise the taste.
source: Turnwald et al., Increasing Vegetable Intake by Emphasizing Tasty and Enjoyable Attributes, Psychological Science 2019

rule: Say the customer's own thing by its name: 'that grey t-shirt', not 'that'.
result: one standard deviation more concrete words = about 9% more satisfaction; e-mails: $32.73 -> $42.80 spent in 90 days (30%), conservative estimate 13%
measured_by: 200 recorded calls and 941 e-mail exchanges of two retailers, plus experiments
fails: observational in the field; very concrete can feel slow when the person wants speed
how_to_use: In the first sentence repeat the buyer's exact object: 'your white oak table', 'the size 43 boots'.
source: Packard & Berger, How Concrete Language Shapes Customer Satisfaction, J. Consumer Research 2021

rule: A person answering for a firm should say 'I', not 'we': 'I can help' sells more afterwards.
result: field: firm agents' 'I' raised customers' later purchases, 'we' and 'you' did not; experiments repeat it
measured_by: over 1,200 real customer e-mail exchanges plus experiments
fails: field part is correlational
how_to_use: Replies and first lines from a named person: 'I have set it aside for you', never 'We have received your enquiry'.
source: Packard, Moore, McFerran, (I'm) Happy to Help (You), J. Marketing Research 2018 (SFU copy)

rule: 'I recommend it' moves others more than 'I liked it' - and it is beginners who say it.
result: explicit recommendations more likely to change what others choose; novices used them 58.0% of the time vs fewer for experts
measured_by: lab and field language studies (N in paper)
fails: 60% of those who chose the worse wine recommended it: the word is not proof of quality
how_to_use: Ask happy customers for the sentence 'I recommend ...' and print that, with the expert's name beside it.
source: Packard & Berger, How Language Shapes Word of Mouth's Impact, J. Marketing Research 2017

rule: The slogan people like best is not the one that works; the one tied to a thing they meet daily is.
result: liked 4.11 vs 1.91, believed stronger 3.54 vs 2.27; only the ugly one changed eating (+25%)
measured_by: N = 59 plus a 35-person pretest
fails: small sample
how_to_use: Never choose the line by asking which one people like.
source: Berger & Fitzsimons, Dogs on the Street, Pumas on Your Feet, J. Marketing Research 2008

rule: Show one example, not a table of four, and do not tell the reader what to use it for.
result: one example raised take-up as much as a 25% cut in price
measured_by: 53,194 letters randomised, consumer lender; method only - the product is outside our line
holds: direct mail offer to past customers
fails: a competitor comparison and many other 'clever' features did nothing
how_to_use: In an offer letter print one worked example with one price.
source: Bertrand, Karlan, Mullainathan, Shafir, Zinman, What's Advertising Content Worth?, QJE 2010

rule: A sender's picture plus 'when will you do it' line beat a letter with every trick in it.
result: letter with picture + plan prompt: +13.17% enrolments; 'kitchen sink' letter with all techniques: +1.84%
measured_by: SBST, health insurance letters, n = 744,510
how_to_use: Pick two devices: the writer's real photo, and a line for the date; leave the rest out.
source: Social and Behavioral Sciences Team, 2015 Annual Report (White House)

rule: 'Please' helped a subject line and the exclamation mark hurt; lunchtime beat early morning.
result: 'Please' vs 'Take it Today': +1.0 point clicks, +0.5 opens; exclamation mark: -0.8 opens, -0.5 clicks; 11:55 a.m. 15.3% clicks vs 13.3% at 8:55
measured_by: SBST/GSA randomised e-mail test, office workers
how_to_use: No exclamation mark in a subject line; say please; send before lunch.
source: Social and Behavioral Sciences Team, 2015 Annual Report (White House)

rule: Longer is sometimes better: when the reader must understand a benefit, the longer e-mail got more finished applications.
measured_by: SBST/Federal Student Aid randomised e-mails
holds: borrowers deciding on a repayment plan
fails: a plain request: the short e-mail wins (4.8% vs 2.7%)
how_to_use: Short for a request; as long as needed to explain a real gain.
source: Social and Behavioral Sciences Team, 2015 Annual Report (White House)

rule: A short address line makes people act online.
result: short web address on the letter: online payments 1.49% -> 2.16% (+45%)
measured_by: SBST/Treasury randomised, n = 21,305
fails: total payments did not rise (p not given here)
how_to_use: On paper print one short address, nothing else to type.
source: Social and Behavioral Sciences Team, 2015 Annual Report (White House)

rule: What you lose by doing nothing beat what you gain, and a set hour to call beat both.
result: consequences of inaction: 41% more calls than benefits; a specific appointment time: +61% on top
measured_by: SBST/Education, borrowers in default, 65,000 in second test
fails: tax letters: no difference
how_to_use: State the real loss in line one, put the hour in line two.
source: Social and Behavioral Sciences Team, 2016 Annual Report (White House)

rule: '72 hours' opens a little better than '3 days'.
result: 8.0% vs 7.7% opened
measured_by: SBST, health insurance deadline e-mails
fails: tiny difference; sign-ups not read
how_to_use: Only with a true deadline; write hours in the last three days.
source: Social and Behavioral Sciences Team, 2016 Annual Report (White House)

rule: Putting a 'Donate' button on the banner cut clicks; a 'Read now' button raised them; plain white beat styled.
result: no percentages printed; picture banners beat text-only by about 50%
measured_by: Wikimedia Foundation live tests 2010
holds: cold readers on a page they came to for something else
fails: 2011: a green natural background beat white (clicks +64%)
how_to_use: First click asks for reading, not for money.
source: Wikimedia Foundation, Fundraising 2010 Report

rule: What made Wikipedia's appeals win: straightforward first line, a person's own words, where the money goes.
result: own list after a year of tests; personal appeals from several people reached the founder's level
measured_by: Wikimedia Foundation, 2011 tests
how_to_use: First line plain and compelling; name exactly what the money does.
source: Wikimedia Foundation, Fundraising 2011 Report

rule: Name the reader's country in the first line.
result: 8 of 10 localised tests up; a reader 11% more likely to give when the opening line named his country
measured_by: Wikimedia Foundation, 10 significant A/B tests
fails: 2 of 10 did not rise
how_to_use: Start with the place: 'To everyone in Norway', 'To our readers in Leeds'.
source: Wikimedia Foundation, Fundraising 2015-16 Report

rule: A charge for the cup works, the same sum as a discount does not.
result: discount: no difference (B = 0.005, n.s.); charge: +3.4 points; messages alone +2.3; selling cups +2.5; giving free cups +4.3
measured_by: 12 university and business cafes, interrupted time series
how_to_use: Print 'Paper cup 25p' rather than '25p off with your own cup'.
source: Poortinga & Whitaker, Promoting the Use of Reusable Coffee Cups, Sustainability 2018

rule: A portrait helps a personal letter and hurts a list of facts.
result: facts banner: 1.6-2.3 times more gifts without the face; personal appeal: face adds up to 30%
measured_by: Wikimedia, several live tests 2012
how_to_use: Decide first: letter from a person (face) or the facts (no face). Never both.
source: Wikimedia Foundation fund-raising team, Fundraising 2012/We Need A Breakthrough (public test diary, May-November 2012)

rule: Naming a small sum brings many small givers; showing the average gift lifts the amount.
result: average $20 shown: $13,626 vs $10,326 with nearly the same gifts (910 vs 874); elsewhere 790 vs 856
measured_by: Wikimedia, October 2012
fails: mixed between banners
how_to_use: On the order page show the true average order; keep the small sum for the first line.
source: Wikimedia Foundation fund-raising team, Fundraising 2012/We Need A Breakthrough (public test diary, May-November 2012)

rule: Highlighting 'we run on YOUR donations' or moving the strongest line to the centre did not win; shortening the facts lost.
result: 'you' 298 vs 310; centred 331 vs 381 and 34 vs 57; shorter bar 478 vs 548 and 336 vs 375
measured_by: Wikimedia, November 2012
how_to_use: Do not assume 'you' or fewer words wins: test; the facts carried the gift.
source: Wikimedia Foundation fund-raising team, Fundraising 2012/We Need A Breakthrough (public test diary, May-November 2012)

rule: Of nine nudge letters to nearly a million people only two moved anything: a new benefit, and sending it twice.
result: +0.89 and +0.73 points; the rest not significant
measured_by: 964,870 people, Denmark
fails: base rate already 80%
how_to_use: Bring news and repeat; most clever wordings do nothing.
source: Johansen et al., Electronic nudges to increase influenza vaccination uptake in Denmark (NUDGE-FLU), The Lancet 2023 (abstract)

rule: Making the winning facts shorter, bigger and prettier lost almost a third of the gifts.
result: 483 vs 699 gifts ('fewer words and vertical lines'); shorter bars also lost in Canada and Australia
measured_by: Wikimedia, 20 September and 24-25 November 2012
fails: after the click a shorter appeal did better (1,478 vs 1,374)
how_to_use: Keep every fact that earns in the first box; shorten what repeats it afterwards.
source: Wikimedia Foundation fund-raising team, Fundraising 2012/We Need A Breakthrough (public test diary, May-November 2012)

rule: The banner that carries the facts beat the founder's face three to four times in October 2012.
result: Canada 375 vs 108 and 320 vs 106 gifts; Britain 474 vs 145 and 142; Australia/New Zealand 259 vs 100
measured_by: Wikimedia live tests, repeated in four regions
holds: the same organisation, two years after the face won everything
how_to_use: A winner wears out: every season put the old winner against a new kind.
source: Wikimedia Foundation fund-raising team, Fundraising 2012/We Need A Breakthrough (public test diary, May-November 2012)

rule: A neighbour comparison on the bill moves behaviour a little and for long; it must also praise those who do well.
result: 2.0% less electricity on average, 6% among the heaviest users, near zero among the lightest; equal to an 11-20% price rise
measured_by: OPOWER natural field experiments, 600,000 households
fails: small effect; lightest users do not move
how_to_use: Give each customer his own measured rank, and a smile to the best.
source: Allcott, Social norms and energy conservation, J. Public Economics 2011

rule: A sale sign sells even without a lower price, but every further sign on the page weakens it.
result: one sign alone: demand for that item up 17% on average with five items on the page; only 3% if one other item also has a sign
measured_by: catalogue field and panel data, several studies
fails: true sale only, else it deceives
how_to_use: One honest 'sale' per screen; never a page of red stickers.
source: Anderson & Simester, Are Sale Signs Less Effective When More Products Have Them?, Marketing Science 2001

rule: A $9 ending raised demand in all three catalogue experiments; strongest for new items; weaker beside a 'Sale' sign.
result: increase in all three experiments (figures behind the paywall)
measured_by: Three randomised catalogue tests, women's clothing
fails: figures not seen
how_to_use: Use .9 endings on new items; not together with a sale cue.
source: Anderson & Simester, Effects of $9 Price Endings on Retail Sales, QME 2003 (abstract page)

rule: Scientific proof of effect lifts the big givers and lowers the small ones: match the opening to the size of the customer.
result: no effect on average; larger prior donors gave more, smaller gave less when told of measured effectiveness
measured_by: Freedom from Hunger, 16,889 letters in the first wave
fails: average effect zero
how_to_use: Numbers-and-study opening for business buyers and big spenders; story opening for small ones.
source: Karlan & Wood, The effect of effectiveness, 2014 (JBEE 2016)

rule: Real-world wording changes give about +1.4 points, not the +8.7 the journals print.
result: 126 trials by two nudge units: +1.4 points (8.1% on a 17.2% base); academic papers: +8.7 points (33.5%)
measured_by: All trials of BIT North America and OES, over 23 million people (paper)
how_to_use: Promise a client 5-10% relative lift from a better line, not doubling; test with thousands.
source: DellaVigna & Linos, RCTs to Scale: Comprehensive Evidence from Two Nudge Units, NBER 27594, 2020

rule: On shop pages true stock and true demand messages move money; colours and buttons do not.
result: stock pointer +2.9% revenue per visitor, others' behaviour +2.3%, countdown +1.5%, abandonment +1.1%; colour 0.0%, buttons -0.2%, calls to action -0.3%; 90% of tests under 1.2%
measured_by: Qubit, 6,700 online experiments
fails: countdowns vary widely; only true stock and dates are allowed
how_to_use: Show the real remaining number and the real number bought this week; do not spend tests on button colour.
source: Browne & Swarbrick Jones (Qubit), What works in e-commerce - a meta-analysis of 6700 online experiments, 2017

rule: The best of 53 gym programmes paid a tiny reward for coming back after a missed day.
result: 45% of programmes raised visits by 9-27%; the winner: micro-reward for returning after a miss; nobody predicted it
measured_by: 61,293 members of a gym chain (paper), randomised
fails: only 8% still worked after four weeks
how_to_use: Write the 'come back' line for the lapsed customer before the welcome line.
source: Milkman et al., Megastudies improve the impact of applied behavioural science, Nature 2021

rule: One named person beats a statistic in real mailings, but the laboratory version failed when repeated: use it as a story, not as a law.
result: replication with hypothetical gifts: no support (effect .000); field mailing in India: 0.24% vs 0.09% donors
measured_by: Preregistered replication of Small et al. 2007; HelpAge field experiment 184,396 letters
fails: hypothetical gifts online
how_to_use: Show one person with name and photo; test against facts each time.
source: Maier et al., Revisiting and Rethinking the Identifiable Victim Effect, Collabra 2023

rule: What 100 years of postal tests say: a pen inside, a personal letter, a stamped return envelope, a first notice, brevity; a teaser on the envelope did nothing.
result: odds of reply: pen 1.44, personalised 1.15, stamped return 1.23, notice in advance 1.36, shorter form 1.58, handwritten signature 1.24; envelope teaser 1.08 (not significant), coloured ink 1.16 (n.s.), appeal type 1.06 (n.s.)
measured_by: Cochrane review of randomised trials (e.g. 146 trials, 277,802 people for gifts; 75 trials, 98,285 for personal letters)
fails: surveys, not sales
how_to_use: Spend on the pen, the hand signature and the advance note, not on the envelope slogan.
source: Edwards et al., Methods to increase response to postal and electronic questionnaires, Cochrane review (2023 update)

rule: In e-mail a picture and a brief letter tripled replies; the word 'Survey' in the subject line cut them by a fifth.
result: picture in e-mail OR 3.05; brief letter OR 3.26; simple header 1.23; deadline 1.18; 'Survey' in subject 0.81
measured_by: Cochrane review, randomised trials of e-questionnaires
fails: picture: few trials
how_to_use: Short letter, one picture, a date; never name the chore in the subject line.
source: Edwards et al., Methods to increase response to postal and electronic questionnaires, Cochrane review (2023 update)

rule: 'Reserved for your appointment' did not work everywhere: at UCLA in 2022-23 it changed nothing for the whole list.
result: portal 0.99, text 1.00, pre-appointment reminder 1.01 (adjusted risk ratios); all groups about 47%; a small gain only among those who had an appointment (aRR 1.04, P = .01)
measured_by: Randomised, 262,085 patients
fails: the 2020 winners (+2.8 to +4.6 points) were not repeated at list level
how_to_use: Use 'reserved for you' only for people who really have a booking, and re-test each year.
source: Szilagyi et al., Text vs patient portal messages to improve influenza vaccination coverage, JAMA Internal Medicine 2024

rule: Pay-what-you-want can earn as much as a high price with more buyers; adding 'half goes to charity' to it makes fewer people buy.
result: tour-boat photos: $5 64% bought ($3.20 each passenger), $15 23% ($3.45), pay-what-you-want 55% ($3.50 profit, $6.43 average); amusement park: 8.39% bought with pay-what-you-want vs 4.49% with charity added
measured_by: Field experiments, 60 boat cruises; park riders
holds: souvenir photos at the moment of joy
fails: not for goods with high cost
how_to_use: Offer it for a low-cost keepsake on the spot; leave charity out of that line.
source: Gneezy, Gneezy, Nelson, Brown, Shared Social Responsibility: pay-what-you-want pricing and charitable giving, Science 2010

rule: A price just below the round number sells slightly more and hurts quality not at all: a small effect.
result: purchase g = 0.13 (0.01 to 0.25), price image g = 0.28, quality g = 0.00
measured_by: Preregistered meta-analysis, 69 studies, 362 effects, N = 40,541
fails: interval nearly touches zero
how_to_use: Use it, expect little.
source: Troll, Frankenbach, Friese, Loschelder, A meta-analysis on the effects of just-below versus round prices, J. Consumer Psychology 2023

rule: Letters that offer dealers a privilege with a condition, and a feature women can see, can outsell the whole sales force.
result: more carpet sweepers sold by one-cent letters than fourteen salesmen on the road combined; Bissell came to control some 95 per cent of the trade
measured_by: Hopkins, Bissell sales over two or three years of three schemes a year; N of letters not given
holds: dealer mail, a low-margin durable article, 1890s
fails: ideas for new finishes ran out after two or three years
how_to_use: Open with what the reader is allowed to have and the one condition, never with 'please buy'.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "How I Got My Start in Advertising"
doubt: Own account. Today's Bissell history credits other factors too; not checked.

rule: Move the guarantee to the person the buyer knows and pays, and say it in the first lines.
result: enormous results on one cough cure, then repeated on Dr. Shoop's Restorative and Rheumatic Cure; newspaper spend grew to $400,000 a year
measured_by: Hopkins; tested first on one product, then on others; no counts
holds: products where the buyer doubts the result; three remedies
fails: not tested alone against a maker's guarantee with counts
how_to_use: Open with risk removed and name the local guarantor.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Medical Advertising"
doubt: Patent medicines; no numbers for the split.

rule: Tell the plain facts of how the product is made, even if every rival does the same: whoever tells first owns them.
result: one client (a drink, left out of the library) went from fifth place to neck-and-neck with first place in a very few months; 'again and again' used on other goods (Puffed grains, Van Camp's beans, Goodyear, Mitchell)
measured_by: Hopkins's clients' sales rank; N campaigns not counted
holds: goods alike among makers; he names it as the basis of many other campaigns
fails: his later book warns it must be specific; not split-tested here
how_to_use: Walk through the workshop, write down what surprises an outsider, open with that single fact.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Medical Advertising"
doubt: The best-known number belongs to an alcoholic product, which is left out as a row; own account.

rule: Open with a service or a gift to the reader, never with 'buy mine': the baker, not the seller, asks for the sale.
result: one man, about a week, sold more than six salesmen in six weeks, at a price half a cent a pound over the rival
measured_by: Swift's orders as told by Hopkins; every leading baker in big New England cities bought; N not given
fails: Hopkins says other salesmen could not be taught it
how_to_use: First line: what the reader gets, free and useful, before the product's name.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Personal Salesmanship"
doubt: Own account.

rule: Buying the first package for the reader, announced in the ad, costs little per reply and brings several times its cost in later sales.
result: cost per request 18 cents, sale per request 90 cents in test cities within thirty days; over 1,500,000 requests next year at 18 cents, 91 cents sale; guarantee claims under 2 per cent of sales
measured_by: Hopkins; a dozen small Illinois test cities first, then 1,500,000 requests
holds: a repeat-purchase product; test towns predicted the national numbers to the cent
fails: the product itself was later shown worthless (see doubt): the offer, not the claim, is the lesson
how_to_use: Lead with 'we buy the first one for you', a coupon to a named shop; test it in a few towns first.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "My Liquozone Experience"
doubt: Liquozone was exposed in Collier's 'The Great American Fraud' (1905-06) as a near-worthless liquid: the opening itself is left out of the library because the product's claim deceived.

rule: Show the crowd going to the product, in true figures: people follow the crowd because they cannot judge the goods.
result: used for Overland ('one of the largest-selling cars in the world'), Goodyear ('sensational growth in demand' featured) and Studebaker (150,000 cars a year quoted); Hopkins calls it 'the most effective thing I have ever found in advertising'
measured_by: Hopkins, three campaigns in this book; no split
fails: needs real growth; not separated from other changes
how_to_use: Open with the number who already chose, the place and the speed of growth, all true.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Automobile Advertising"
doubt: Judgment after many campaigns, not a split test.

rule: If the product cannot keep the promise, the better the opening works the faster it ruins the seller.
result: Mitchell: record inquiries and sales, then hundreds of cars came back and recovery proved impossible
measured_by: one company, told by Hopkins
fails: one case
how_to_use: Before writing, prove the claim on the goods; a strong hook is a loan on the product.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Automobile Advertising"
doubt: One case.

rule: Name in every advertisement the shops that stock you: shops then stock you so as not to be left out.
result: in a few months about 30,000 dealers induced to stock Goodyear tires on a $250 minimum
measured_by: Goodyear; 30,000 dealers; no control
holds: local newspaper campaigns; used 'often' on new products
fails: not tested separately
how_to_use: In local video or print, name the shops as the closing line of the opening block.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Tire Advertising"
doubt: Own account.

rule: An appeal that wins in one small town wins from coast to coast, so buy the first proof for a few hundred dollars.
result: a $700 test in one town, $50,000 of tests in numerous towns, 'always with like results'
measured_by: Hopkins, Palmolive 1911; towns not counted
holds: mass goods; repeated in other goods (Pepsodent, puffed grains)
fails: low-priced mass soap only; not tested on expensive goods
how_to_use: Try three openings in three towns or three small audiences before any large spend.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Early History of Palmolive"
doubt: Own account, figures from memory.

rule: Give samples only to people who acted to get them, because an ad made them want it: samples thrown at the door do not make users.
result: millions of promiscuous samples 'did not win many users'; coupons in tens of millions of magazines, requested after reading, did; newspaper advertising at large could not pay on this line
measured_by: Hopkins; Quaker sales, no counts
holds: puffed grains, milk, soap: three categories in this book
fails: newspaper pages reach people who cannot afford an expensive food; use selective media
how_to_use: Let the first line build the wish, then let the reader ask for the sample.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Puffed Grains and Quaker Oats"
doubt: Own account, no figures.

rule: Do not open by trying to change a habit; sell to people who already want the thing, and show them the better way.
result: Quaker's oatmeal-conversion campaign did not pay (a new convert never paid his cost); Pepsodent estimate: a new toothbrush convert costs at least $25; later advertising to existing users 'gained large results'
measured_by: Hopkins; Quaker, hundreds of data men, no counts
fails: a habit shift paid for by free editorial writing, not ads, he says
how_to_use: Choose the opening reader who already does it; write to that reader only.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Puffed Grains and Quaker Oats"
doubt: Hopkins's generalisation; the cost figures are his estimates. Scientific Advertising: tests put a toothbrush convert at $20 to $25.

rule: In health and beauty, do not make 'free' the headline: it cut results to a quarter; offer the test as science, with the free sample only inside.
result: featuring a free offer at the top of the ads divided results by four; asking 10 cents for a sample was almost ignored
measured_by: Pepsodent keyed coupons; hundreds of ads; count for this comparison not given
fails: breakfast food and dessert: there 'free' multiplied readers
how_to_use: For a beauty/health client put the reason first, the free sample in the coupon; for food, put free first.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Pepsodent"
doubt: Own keyed test; N not given.

rule: Show rewards, not penalties: people will not read about disasters, only about success, beauty and cheer.
result: hundreds of keyed ads; beauty the chief appeal; scores of rivals who scared failed, as far as he knows
measured_by: Pepsodent, coupons keyed by ad; 'hundreds of ads'
holds: dental and beauty goods; trouble already present is the exception he names
fails: a trouble already created: appeal to it can work
how_to_use: Open with the person they will become; use a scare only when they already feel the trouble.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Pepsodent"
doubt: Own testing, N of each appeal not given; scare copy worked for others later (halitosis, other hands).

rule: Judgment and experience fail even after thirty years: one series of his own ads would have wrecked Pepsodent in three months; only keyed results show the opening that sells.
result: a million dollars on an account he first refused; mistakes caught in a week
measured_by: Pepsodent coupons, weekly, hundreds of ads
how_to_use: Read weekly which headline brought which cost, and kill the losing opening in a week.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Pepsodent"
doubt: Own account.

rule: Never buy good looks with space: a plain, small ad won with cost per reply of 42 cents against $14.20 for the larger, more alluring ad.
result: old cost per reply 85 cents; larger alluring ad of another agency $14.20; the plain ad 42 cents, kept around 42 cents for years; on 250,000 replies a year
measured_by: keyed replies of a five-dollar mail article; each ad run by the advertiser; about 250,000 replies per year
holds: a five-dollar mail article; 'thousands of tests on hundreds of lines' for the general claim
fails: he names only the one case here
how_to_use: Judge the opening by cost per reply, not by how handsome it looks.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Some Mail-Order Experiences"
doubt: Article not named; the $14.20 ad may also differ in medium and season. Scientific Advertising tells the same case as 41 cents over two years.

rule: Doubling the space with large type or decoration doubles the cost of replies and sales.
result: 'take a profitable mail-order ad, set it in twice the space: you will double the cost of replies and sales'
measured_by: Hopkins: 'thousands of tests' claimed; N not given
fails: print where the goal is not a coupon reply is not tested
how_to_use: Spend words and area on the argument, not on decoration.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Some Mail-Order Experiences"
doubt: Claimed number of tests is not documented; does not carry to video.

rule: Change only the headline and the replies can change eight- to tenfold.
result: 'Again and again I have multiplied results from an ad. by eight or ten by a simple change in headline'; one headline attracts a certain percentage, another ten times as many; one type 25 per cent of prospects, another 50 per cent
measured_by: Hopkins, keyed tests over thirty-six years, hundreds of lines, thousands of pieces of copy compared; N of headline pairs not given
fails: individual pairs are not printed here
how_to_use: Write many headlines for one body and let the coupon choose.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Scientific Advertising"
doubt: Self-reported; no pair documented. Scientific Advertising says five to ten times (see that row).

rule: Exact figures are believed at par; superlatives are discounted.
result: tungsten lamp: 'gives more light' mildly impresses; '3 1/4 times the light of carbon lamps' is accepted as a fact (the numeral in the scan is garbled '314'); used on Palmolive shaving cream (250 times lather), Chalmers (9 per cent profit), garments (3 per cent)
measured_by: Hopkins across several accounts in the book; not a counted test each time
fails: not numbered as a split test here
how_to_use: Replace every adjective in the first line by a number you can prove.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Scientific Advertising"
doubt: Scan garbled '314'; the figure itself is not our claim.

rule: A coupon to cut multiplies replies: the reader keeps it, and it acts later.
result: 'Countless tests have proved that coupons multiply returns'; in catalogue tests by mail-order houses the difference 'was enormous'
measured_by: Hopkins, mail-order houses' tests of ads with and without coupons; N not given
fails: a coupon that asks for money or half price is small inducement (own chapter)
how_to_use: Give the opening something to keep: a code, a card, a save button.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Scientific Advertising"
doubt: No numbers.

rule: Extra art and colour have not paid their cost on any line he traced.
result: no test he knew proved $1,500-$4,000 drawings profitable, nor colour better than black and white; 'a good many comparisons'
measured_by: Hopkins's keyed comparisons; N not given
fails: he allows for fruits and desserts; not applicable to video
how_to_use: Spend on the message first.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising, Harper & Brothers, 1927, ch. "Scientific Advertising"
doubt: A 1927 judgment on print only.

rule: Judge the opening by cost per customer, not by replies: one ad may bring many worthless replies.
result: coupon counts are 'not final'; 'final conclusions are always based on cost per customer or cost per dollar of sale'
measured_by: Lord & Thomas practice: coupon returns on hundreds of lines, thousands of separate ads on a single line
how_to_use: Follow each opening through to the sale before scaling it.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "1 How Advertising Laws Are Established"
doubt: Method statement; no pair of numbers.

rule: A striking picture bought with extra space can bring not one added sale.
result: 50 percent more space for a row of chickens in silhouette raised the cost per reply by exactly 50 percent and brought not one added sale
measured_by: keyed incubator ad, type only against ad with picture; N not given
holds: practical buyers of incubators; line not matched by a right headline
fails: he does not claim it for goods people buy with their eyes (a dress picture may occupy much space)
how_to_use: Put the picture in only if it shows the thing sold and cheaper per reply.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "4 Mail Order Advertising"
doubt: Single case.

rule: Tell the whole story when the goal is an immediate sale: 'The more you tell the more you sell'.
result: 'it has never failed to prove out so in any test we know'; an ad twice larger brings twice the returns, four times larger four times 'and usually some in addition' when the space is used as well as the small space
measured_by: Hopkins/Lord & Thomas tests; N not given
fails: half-page copy set in a page doubles the cost of returns
how_to_use: Size the piece to the amount of useful story you have.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "4 Mail Order Advertising"
doubt: Claim of 'never failed' with no counts.

rule: Change the headline and returns change five to ten times over, with the body left alone.
result: 'It is not uncommon for a change in headlines to multiply returns from five to ten times over'; keyed returns on nearly two thousand headlines on one product; stories nearly identical
measured_by: Hopkins/Lord & Thomas: keyed coupon returns on nearly two thousand headlines used on a single product (the product is beauty, disease prevention, cleanliness: read as Pepsodent or a soap [mine])
holds: a product with many uses; print
fails: which headlines won is not printed here
how_to_use: Do not pick the headline by taste: write dozens, key them, read the returns.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "5 Headlines"
doubt: Single firm's records, not published; winners not listed.

rule: Half the winning appeal may still be profitable, so run several headlines in different magazines, one for each kind of reader.
result: if using twenty magazines, they may use twenty separate ads; one appeal may bring half the returns of another 'yet be important enough to be profitable'
measured_by: Hopkins; N not given
how_to_use: Do not force one hook on all audiences: match hooks to the audience they call.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "5 Headlines"
doubt: Practice, not a counted test.

rule: Coupons can be cut out by one reader in five when the headline calls them.
result: 'Again and again we see 20 percent of all the readers of a newspaper cut out a certain coupon'
measured_by: Hopkins/Lord & Thomas coupon returns; N not given
fails: not every product
how_to_use: Set a reply target to compare an opening with; expect a hook that asks for a coupon to beat plain reading.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "5 Headlines"
doubt: Own account; the base count (readers) is not documented.

rule: Cheapness is not a strong appeal, and a high price can make people look twice.
result: the British National Gallery painting first passed by, then surrounded once its $750,000 cost was read; $100,000 paid for a formula 'when tried has won a wealth of respect'
measured_by: observation; $100,000 claim 'when tried' is a keyed claim, N not given
fails: not a sales figure
how_to_use: Say the true cost in the first line.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "6 Psychology"
doubt: 'when tried' without counts; the cost must be true.

rule: 'Come and pay me later' beats 'money back if you don't like it', by what he calls many times.
result: 'Pay in a week if you like them' 'proved many times as impressive' than 'try it for a week, we return your money'
measured_by: Hopkins; N not given
fails: on credit: not for payments with interest
how_to_use: Reverse the risk in the opening: the customer keeps the money.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "6 Psychology"
doubt: No count; a trial offer only, no interest.

rule: An offer limited to a certain class of people is far more effective than a general offer.
result: 'far more effective' (veterans, a lodge, executives); no number
measured_by: Hopkins; 'it is found'; N not given
fails: no count
how_to_use: Open with who is entitled: 'Only for teachers of this school'.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "6 Psychology"
doubt: No number; keep the class true.

rule: Put every claim that tested well into every ad: one claim per ad loses a percentage, and serials almost never connect.
result: 'Single mail order ads often run year after year without diminishing returns'; best advertisers accumulate claims by comparing headlines
measured_by: Hopkins; keyed returns; N not given
fails: one-sentence lines suit chewing gum or Cream of Wheat, he says
how_to_use: Hook with one claim, then carry all the tested claims in the body.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "8 Tell Your Full Story"
doubt: No numbers.

rule: The picture that shows the product itself in its curious state sells better than people or scenery.
result: Puffed Grains: pictures of the grains found most effective, no figure drawings compare in results with these grains; Arrow Collars and correspondence-school pictures also 'proved most convincing' in traced ads
measured_by: Hopkins; Puffed grains ad tests; N not given
holds: foods with a curious look; clothes; school ads; beauty ads (beautiful people)
fails: eccentric pictures cost sales; incubator chickens added nothing
how_to_use: Open the video on the product in its odd, true state.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "9 Art In Advertising"
doubt: No counts.

rule: Colour pays for foods that look better in colour (oranges, desserts), and not generally.
result: tests on lines like oranges, desserts show that colour pays; not generally, by evidence gathered to date
measured_by: Hopkins; tests of the 1910s-20s; N not given
holds: foods that look far better in colour
fails: most other lines; print
how_to_use: Colour the first frame only if it puts the product on exhibition.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "9 Art In Advertising"
doubt: 1923 print colour costs.

rule: Beauty promise outpulls decay warning by many times for tooth paste; pick the appeal that most readers share.
result: a heading may bring ten times the results of another heading; a tooth paste's beauty appeal 'many times as strong' as decay prevention; eczema claim might reach one in a hundred, beauty nearly all
measured_by: tests (keyed headlines) of 'the most successful tooth paste advertiser', who never features tooth troubles in headlines; N not given
fails: a narrow sickness product where few suffer
how_to_use: Open on beauty for a health product with a general audience; fear only if the trouble is already there.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "10 Things Too Costly"
doubt: Numbers of the tests are not printed ('many times').

rule: The word 'Free' multiplies the readers of most ads, and a price on a sample raises the cost of the reply.
result: ten cents asked for a sample may add from 40 cents to $1 to the cost of replies; some ads on the same product cost ten times what others cost
measured_by: Hopkins; keyed samples; 'may'
fails: hygiene and beauty goods (Pepsodent: 'free' at the top cut results to a quarter)
how_to_use: Test 'free' in food, gadget, gift openings; not in health and beauty.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "13 Use of Samples"
doubt: 'May' figures; My Life gives the 4:1 contradiction for hygiene. My Life: free sample inquiries 25 cents each, ten-cent samples $1.25 or more, perhaps one-fifth as many users (illustration).

rule: Where the sample can be fetched decides the cost of the reply: at the local shop about 18-22 cents, by mail 70 cents.
result: mail sample inquiries 70 cents each; same ads, coupon presented at a local store 18 to 22 cents; often four times as many present a coupon at a store as mail it
measured_by: Hopkins; 'on a line before the writer now', keyed; N not given
holds: foods and household goods in cities with local stores
fails: goods without local stock
how_to_use: End the hook on the nearest shop, not on a form.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "13 Use of Samples"
doubt: One line, N not printed.

rule: Give the choice of the easiest reply: on one line 70 percent came by telephone, not by post or visit.
result: Seventy percent of the inquiries came by telephone (three methods offered: write, phone, call at a store)
measured_by: one line's inquiries; N not given
fails: not a comparison of wording
how_to_use: Offer tap-to-call first.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "13 Use of Samples"
doubt: N not given; channel, not words.

rule: Half price or 'buy one, get one' offers do not bring new users: it is as hard to get half price as full price before the reader is converted.
result: 'Any keyed returns will clearly prove that such offers do not pay'
measured_by: Hopkins; keyed; N not given
fails: not tested for repeat buyers
how_to_use: Keep discounts out of the hook for strangers.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "13 Use of Samples"
doubt: No numbers. My Life: tens of millions of ads offering Puffed Wheat free with Puffed Rice brought few new users.

rule: Published evaporated-milk coupon: 1,460,000 requests in one issue, from one paper day in Greater New York; a chocolate drink had one coupon in five presented.
result: 1,460,000 requests; one-fifth of the coupons presented on a chocolated drink
measured_by: Hopkins; coupons redeemed
fails: a less used line brings a fraction
how_to_use: Estimate the reply to a free-pack opening before choosing it.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "13 Use of Samples"
doubt: Same event as the Van Camp row in My Life. SA says they do NOT announce the date of such coupon offers; My Life says it was announced three weeks ahead: the two books differ.

rule: Trying plan after plan lowers the cost: fifty plans in five years for one food made advertising four times more effective.
result: over fifty separate plans in five years; the best reduced cost of selling by 75 percent
measured_by: one food advertiser, test towns; N not given
fails: the winning plan is not described
how_to_use: Budget tests for life, not only for launch.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "15 Test Campaigns"
doubt: Own account; the plans (not only headlines) changed.

rule: What a thousand customers cost tells what a million will cost, if the small test is fair.
result: tests in four or five towns cost $3,000 to $5,000; nearly every test brought back its cost in time; largest accounts built this way
measured_by: Hopkins/Lord & Thomas; number of tests not given
fails: premium goods that need selective media
how_to_use: Set the test size so that the cost per customer is known before the spend.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "15 Test Campaigns"
doubt: 'almost exactly' without counts; survivors only.

rule: A new form of a food was judged by mail in a few towns: one voted down, one voted 91 percent yes.
result: first form: users almost unanimous in disapproval; second form: 91 percent of a few thousand women voted for it; tests cost about $1,000 each
measured_by: a large food advertiser; a few thousand women; free package by coupon, then a letter
fails: two new products only
how_to_use: Ask buyers about the thing itself before the hook.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "15 Test Campaigns"
doubt: Same as Quick Quaker in My Life, where the scan says about 90 percent ('go').

rule: The bright side outpulls the dark side four to one.
result: the positive ad outpulls the other four to one, 'if you have our experience'
measured_by: Hopkins; two ads, one negative one positive; N not given
holds: his clients: tooth paste, beauty, business schools, clothes
fails: fear can win when the trouble exists (his own exception in My Life); other hands' tests may differ
how_to_use: Open with the goal, not the penalty; test the dark line only for people who already have the trouble.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "18 Negative Advertising"
doubt: Own rule of thumb; no table; conflicts with loss-framing results found by other researchers.

rule: Test twenty-five letters on a thousand prospects each before mailing millions, and mail the one that pays.
result: a magazine mailing millions of letters a year: twenty-five letters, each with a thousand prospects; letter which pays best is used
measured_by: one magazine publisher; 25 x 1,000
how_to_use: Same for e-mail subjects: 25 openings, 1,000 readers each.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "19 Letter Writing"
doubt: Describes practice; results not printed.

rule: Plain stationery replies as well as fine, and fine pamphlets lessen the effect.
result: two-cent letter gets no more attention than a one-cent letter; fine stationery no more than poor; fine pamphlets lessen
measured_by: 'Experience generally shows', letters tested; N not given
fails: N not given
how_to_use: Spend on the first line and the offer.
source: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising, 1923, ch. "19 Letter Writing"
doubt: No numbers; today's envelope tests by others differ.

rule: Testing many small changes of the same opening in different regions, with a sample coupon as the meter, can carry an unknown brand to first place without salesmen.
result: sales $200,000 in the first year to $6 million by 1922; No. 1 selling toothpaste within 18 months of its first national advertisement
measured_by: company sales reported by a museum history; N of ads 'a massive variety'
fails: growth stalled on the home market by 1927-29 under competition; the claim was judged unfounded by dentists
how_to_use: Run the same body with slightly changed copy in different places, meter with a free trial.
source: Made-in-Chicago Museum, 'Pepsodent Company, est. 1915'
doubt: Museum article without footnote for these figures in the passage; spend also very large; product claim misled (Gies).

rule: Say plainly what is inside: the poetic, clever or learned title loses to the one that tells what you get.
result: Fourteen retitled books printed with before/after figures, from near zero to 7,000-30,000 copies a year; he states no poetic title that won
measured_by: Haldeman-Julius: yearly mail-order copies of the same books under different titles; 1,260 titles, more than 400 changed in title or listing
holds: One-line offers where the line must sell alone: catalogue, list, price tag, feed caption.
fails: Famous titles (Shakespeare, Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde) must not be touched; he had no figures on length.
how_to_use: First rule: make the line describe the thing with one dominant word; second: make it distinctive. In that order.
source: E. Haldeman-Julius, The First Hundred Million (Simon and Schuster, 1928), ch. VIII "The Hospital", p. 160
doubt: Before/after by years; he chose which examples to print; he names failures too.

rule: Certain words lift sales in title after title: Truth, Life, Love, How to, Facts You Should Know, The Story of.
result: Truth: 3,000 to 10,000; How to: 0 to 30,000; The Story of: 10,000 to 45,000
measured_by: Haldeman-Julius: yearly mail-order copies of the same books under different titles; 1,260 titles, more than 400 changed in title or listing
fails: "Facts About the Moon" was weaker than "Is the Moon a Dead World?": no word works everywhere.
how_to_use: Write one version of the line with each of these words and test them against each other.
source: E. Haldeman-Julius, The First Hundred Million (Simon and Schuster, 1928), ch. VIII "The Hospital", p. 160
doubt: Before/after by years; he chose which examples to print; he names failures too.

rule: The thing interests people more than the person behind it.
result: Einstein 15,000 to 42,000; Nietzsche 10,000 to 45,000; Bernhardt 14,000 to 29,500; The Facts About Fascism 24,000 against The Truth About Mussolini 14,000
measured_by: Haldeman-Julius: yearly mail-order copies of the same books under different titles; 1,260 titles, more than 400 changed in title or listing
fails: Very famous names (Lincoln, Napoleon) sell on "Life of".
how_to_use: Open with what the expert found or makes, then his name.
source: E. Haldeman-Julius, The First Hundred Million (Simon and Schuster, 1928), ch. IX "What a Change of Scenery Will Do", p. 175
doubt: Before/after by years; he chose which examples to print; he names failures too.

rule: The heading under which a thing is placed sells it as much as its own name.
result: Same book 2,000 to 16,000, 7,000 to 21,000, 1,500 to 6,000 after a move of heading
measured_by: Haldeman-Julius: yearly mail-order copies of the same books under different titles; 1,260 titles, more than 400 changed in title or listing
holds: Catalogues, menus, shop shelves, playlists, page sections.
fails: Not separated from title changes in several examples.
how_to_use: Re-test a weak offer under another heading (Humor, How to, Famous Women) before dropping it; never "Miscellaneous".
source: E. Haldeman-Julius, The First Hundred Million (Simon and Schuster, 1928), ch. IX "What a Change of Scenery Will Do", p. 170
doubt: Before/after by years; he chose which examples to print; he names failures too.

rule: Readers of very different magazines buy almost the same things: one human nature, so the same opening travels.
result: Same list run in seven publications; 500 good sellers could be advertised in all seven without change of emphasis and get substantially the same results
measured_by: Haldeman-Julius: copies per 1,000 orders in Harper's, Nation, Smart Set, Pathfinder, N.Y. Times Book Review, Liberty, N.Y. Graphic (1927)
holds: Mass offers at a low price.
fails: Women's magazines and small-city newspapers never paid for him; Pathfinder (small towns) differed.
how_to_use: Do not write a different hook for each class of reader first; test the same winner everywhere, then adjust.
source: E. Haldeman-Julius, The First Hundred Million (1928), ch. XVI, p. 321
doubt: Before/after by years; he chose which examples to print; he names failures too.

rule: A closing date draws fast action, but only a true one, and it stops pulling the day after.
result: Eight years of date-line pages paid out; plain copy without a date "never paid out" until late 1927; then plain list took $320 against $265
measured_by: Haldeman-Julius: keyed advertisements, Chicago Tribune first-day returns and nine years of campaigns
holds: Unknown product, low price, mail order.
fails: Established reputation: the plain list beat the closing date in 1928.
how_to_use: Use a real deadline while the name is unknown; retire it once the name sells by itself.
source: E. Haldeman-Julius, The First Hundred Million (1928), ch. XV p. 279, ch. XVII
doubt: Before/after by years; he chose which examples to print; he names failures too.

rule: The promise of practical self-improvement sells almost as widely as the strongest subjects, in every class of reader.
result: How to Improve Your Conversation 77,000; Vocabulary 76,000; Etiquette 72,000; minimum to stay in the list 10,000
measured_by: E. Haldeman-Julius: 1,156 mail orders for 25,000 books picked from 1,260 titles at one price, converted to yearly sales (20.7 million books in 1927)
fails: "How to Work Your Way Through College" about 10,000; formal courses are not finished.
how_to_use: Offer one social or practical gain the person can get alone; avoid school words (rhetoric, composition).
source: E. Haldeman-Julius, The First Hundred Million (Simon and Schuster, 1928), ch. III pp. 42-43
doubt: Different books, not only different words.

rule: Letters that lasted lean on one strong feeling, most often flattery: the reader is made to feel well about himself in the first lines.
result: 42% of 1,127 successful direct mail letters were pinned to flattery
measured_by: Axel Andersson, hand count of 1,127 letters in the Who's Mailing What! archive
holds: Subscriptions, memberships, clubs, charities by mail.
fails: A count of what was mailed, not a test against other feelings.
how_to_use: Open by naming something true and good the reader has done or is.
source: Denny Hatch, Marketing Blog #107, 2020
doubt: The archive holds lasting letters, so the count describes winners only.

rule: In a letter to busy people, asking straight out in the first sentence beat the question, the news, the sensation and the sympathy.
result: 4.3% against 3.3% (news), 2.3% (question), under 2% (sensation), under 2% (sympathy)
measured_by: J. C. Aspley, same letter, five openings, 1,000 manufacturers each
holds: Business letters offering a book on approval.
fails: One test, one offer; a news start came second.
how_to_use: Test a first line that simply asks for the small next step.
source: J. C. Aspley, Hundred Point Sales Letters (1921), p. 10
doubt: 1,000 per cell: 4.3 against 3.3 is within chance; against under 2 it is not.

rule: Getting to the point at once multiplied the same arguments.
result: 17 percent against 3 percent, same list and same talking points
measured_by: Edgar W. Jordan for Murray's Roach Doom, 5,000 hospitals
fails: Not tested on entertainment or stories.
how_to_use: Cut everything before the claim and start there.
source: J. C. Aspley, Hundred Point Sales Letters (1921), p. 10

rule: The expert's dislike does not predict the result: letters condemned by professionals won.
result: 12 percent replies after three advertising men advised not to use it; another condemned letter was one of the biggest pullers of its house; record letters "infinitely less clever" than mediocre ones
measured_by: companies quoted in Letters That Make Good (1913)
fails: Anecdotes, not counted.
how_to_use: Mail a test before anyone votes on taste.
source: Letters That Make Good (1913), pp. 91, 97, 117

rule: A changed headline alone can multiply inquiries six times; a fact with a number and the name of the reader's group did it.
result: six times the inquiries (Build Your Own House in Two Hours); inquiry cost to 34 cents from over a dollar (The Deaf Now Hear Whispers)
measured_by: Printers' Ink 1912 cases in Starch (1914)
how_to_use: Keep the ad, change only the line; put in a true astonishing number or the reader's name for himself.
source: Daniel Starch, Advertising (1914), pp. 153-154
doubt: Advertisers anonymous.

rule: Reporting actual happenings with a news headline pulls twice what enthusiastic assertion does.
result: twice as well
measured_by: one test by the 'Schoolmaster' of Printers' Ink, June 1913; N not given
fails: "Maybe the result should not be taken as an invariable rule."
how_to_use: Open with what happened to one named case, as news.
source: Daniel Starch, Advertising (1914), p. 234
doubt: N not given.

rule: Admitting a weakness first makes the rest believed, and it sold.
result: Volkswagen 120,000 (1959) to 430,000 (1967) in a shrinking import market; Avis from loss to profit in a year
measured_by: US sales and company accounts
holds: A true, harmless weakness of a good product.
fails: Not tested against a rival ad; both had other changes.
how_to_use: Write the truest complaint customers make, as the headline, and answer it in the first line.
source: J. Blackburn, JAS 51
doubt: Campaign level.

rule: An object inside the mailing raises response, but the people it brings stay less.
result: 1.27% against 0.66% with a pen (2 x 38,000); 10.04% with a torn exercise book; agency veteran says drop-off is higher
measured_by: Friends of the Earth split test 1999; NSPCC; Ken Burnett's judgement
holds: Charity mail; warm and cold lists.
fails: Long-term value; complaints.
how_to_use: Prefer an object that carries the cause (the torn book, the tea bag) to a plain gift.
source: Third Sector, 2003
doubt: The drop-off part is opinion.

rule: The winner depends on the goal: the envelope that brings more people may bring smaller gifts.
result: Mask envelope: nearly 10 percent more responses; plain invitation: average gift nearly $1 higher and lower cost per dollar
measured_by: envelope split test, National Museum of the American Indian, 1991
how_to_use: Decide first whether you count people or money, then pick the hook.
source: Jacobowitz & Lautman
Motion, Creative Benchmarks 2026
rule: Most new Meta ads lose: plan for roughly one winner in 10 to 25 ads, not for one perfect hook.
result: Winner share by monthly spend: <$10K 4.03 %, $10-50K 6.47 %, $50-200K 8.13 %, $200K-1M 8.64 %, $1M+ 8.80 %; 50-53 % of ads are off before 28 days; winners take about 55 % of spend
measured_by: Motion (sells the analytics tool), 578,750 Meta ads, 6,015 advertisers, $1.29B advertisers own money, launched 1 Sep 2025-1 Jan 2026; winner = spend at least 10x the account median AND at least $500; no control group
fails: Outcome is spend, not sales; other seasons untested
how_to_use: Quote the client a testing volume (about 25-57 openings for a 90 % chance of one winner, our own arithmetic) instead of one hook
doubt: spend is a proxy chosen by Meta delivery and by the buyer

measured_by: Motion, 578,750 Meta ads tagged by AI, same window; hit rate = winners / ads, accounts equal weight; no control

how_to_use: First cut of a sales hook: put the real news, the real price or the real deadline in the first line; use confession and curiosity as the second family

source: Motion, Creative Benchmarks 2026
rule: Give-away, price anchor, announcement, offer, confession, urgency and curiosity openings pull more budget than their share of ads; reasons-why and storytelling pull less.

measured_by: Motion, as above; spend-use ratio; N per family not printed except share of ads (giveaway 0.07 %, price anchor 0.11 %, offer only 8.92 %, urgency 8.62 %, curiosity 5.34 %)

how_to_use: Trust offer, urgency, curiosity and confession (each over 1 % of ads); treat giveaway and price anchor as promising
